#5023. US data center restrictions could give Bitcoin miners an edge in AI, though challenges remain

As US voters push back against new data centers, Bitcoin miners already expanding into AI could benefit from their existing facilities.

Bitcoin miners with power already secured could have an edge in the race to build AI data centers after voters in several US communities backed limits on new development. The midterms could also bring closer scrutiny from Congress over who pays for the grid upgrades those facilities need, industry experts told Cointelegraph.

Voters in several states weighed in on data center development during the Nov. 3 US midterms, when local measures appeared on the same ballots as congressional races. Amid concerns about rising electricity costs, water use and the impact on nearby communities, voters favored limiting development in 40 of the 41 local contests tracked by Ballotpedia.

The restrictions include citywide bans, limits on larger facilities, temporary pauses on new projects and voter approval requirements for some developments.

The results come as major Bitcoin mining companies continue moving into AI, a transition Jamie Brown, CEO of Global Kiwi Labs, said could become more attractive as local restrictions make it harder to build new data centers.

“If a Bitcoin miner has not yet repurposed their electric contract and physical plant to AI, the case to do so just got more compelling,” said Brown, whose company hosts servers for crypto exchanges and trading firms.

Related: US midterm elections 2026 as it happened: Democrats win control of Congress

Miners’ shift to AI infrastructure is already underway, with publicly listed Bitcoin miners announcing more than $70 billion in AI and advanced computing contracts during 2025 and early 2026, according to a first-quarter report by CoinShares.

But state and local decisions can have a more immediate impact on whether data center projects move forward. That’s because local authorities often oversee zoning and building permits and can influence access to electricity.

“A company might have access to an attractive site and a significant amount of power capacity, but if local restrictions prevent it from expanding or upgrading that infrastructure, the opportunity becomes much more difficult to pursue,” said Jordan Knecht, head of strategic integrations at Kresus, a blockchain infrastructure company.

Last week, voters backed 27 measures to limit or oppose new data centers in the elections, according to Ballotpedia. These included five complete bans, 12 partial bans and six-month pauses on new projects in three Maine towns.

In Grove City, Ohio, voters approved a rule requiring public approval for large projects that use more than 20 megawatts of electricity, among other conditions.

“Federal policy will certainly influence the broader investment environment, but the practical ability to develop and operate these facilities often comes down to conditions in individual markets,” Knecht told Cointelegraph. “For miners looking to transition into AI, I think understanding those local dynamics will be just as important as following developments in Washington.”

Building AI-ready data center infrastructure can cost between $8 million and $15 million per megawatt, compared with $700,000 to $1 million per megawatt for traditional mining facilities, according to a 2026 report by CoinShares.

That gap helps explain why a site with power already secured is only a starting point for miners moving into AI. “Transitioning from Bitcoin mining to AI workloads requires significant additional investment in infrastructure for cooling, networking, and reliability,” Knecht said.

Yuliya Barabash, founder of SBSB Fintech Lawyers, also pointed to differences in electricity needs between Bitcoin mining and AI data centers. Bitcoin miners can often reduce electricity use when prices rise, while AI data centers typically need a consistent power supply, she said.

“Higher electricity prices and additional regulatory requirements could make some projects less profitable or delay their implementation,” Barabash told Cointelegraph.

This comes as electricity demand from US data centers is also expected to rise, according to the International Energy Agency (IEA). The agency estimates that data centers used 224 terawatt-hours of electricity in 2025, a figure projected to nearly double to 426 terawatt-hours by 2030.

One question facing the incoming Democratic-controlled Congress is who should pay to expand the grid for large data centers.

Knecht said lawmakers could take a closer look at how those projects affect electricity costs and how they get approved. “There may be more pressure to ensure that large data center operators are paying their fair share of infrastructure costs rather than passing those expenses on to consumers.”

Barabash also expects scrutiny of who pays for the electricity infrastructure needed to support data centers. “One of the key priorities is likely to be ensuring that technology companies, rather than ordinary consumers, bear the costs of the additional electricity infrastructure their facilities require,” she said.

Still, experts noted that closer attention does not necessarily mean Congress will discourage data center development. “AI infrastructure is becoming increasingly important to the US economy, and there is still a strong incentive to support investment in domestic computing capacity,” Knecht said.

For miners weighing a conversion, the question is whether AI revenue can justify the cost of upgrading cooling, networking and power systems. Brown thinks it can. “Miners will swap to AI because it is a better ROI than mining,” he said.

#5022. DTCC to Bring Tokenized Stocks and Treasuries to Solana in 2027

DTCC to Bring Tokenized Stocks and Treasuries to Solana in 2027

The Depository Trust & Clearing Corporation (DTCC), the backbone of U.S. securities settlement, plans to bring its tokenized securities to Solana, it announced on Thursday.

The firm will connect the DTCC Tokenization Service (DTS) to the Solana network, allowing eligible assets held by its Depository Trust Company (DTC) subsidiary to be converted into tokens on Solana. The integration is planned for the second half of 2027.

BREAKING: @The_DTCC to tokenize custodied assets on Solana. announced plans to connect the DTCC Tokenization Service to Solana, enabling the tokenization of eligible DTC-custodied assets on the network.

The integration is planned for the second half of 2027, further advancing… pic.twitter.com/gXszWFgUOX

"DTCC is bringing regulated, DTC-tokenized securities to another major blockchain ecosystem, giving market participants greater choice in where they access and utilize tokenized assets," DTCC CEO Frank La Salla said.

DTS went live on October 28 on the Canton Network and DTCC's own private blockchain, built on the Besu framework, with more networks due to be added in 2027, according to DTCC's launch announcement. The service creates tokenized "digital twins" of securities held at DTC, which custodies more than $114 trillion in assets. Solana joins Stellar and Circle's Arc blockchain, which are expected to be added in 2027, according to a DTCC fact sheet.

Under a no-action letter from the SEC, the service is limited to a defined set of highly liquid assets, including Russell 1000 stocks, ETFs tracking major indexes, and U.S. Treasuries. Morgan Stanley said last week it had tokenized U.S. stocks and Treasuries through the service.

Tokens issued on Solana "will retain the same investor protections, ownership rights and regulatory safeguards that apply to traditionally held securities," said Brian Steele, president of DTCC Clearing & Securities Services.

Solana has been actively courting traditional finance in recent months, with Solana Foundation head of institutional Nick Ducoff arguing that, "Institutions choose Solana because it already runs real financial activity at scale." He added that institutions are "already issuing, settling and deploying capital" on the network, in a tweet shared by Solana's official account.

Last month, the Solana Foundation unveiled an open standard for institutional settlement developed with input from J.P. Morgan, and the network completed its Alpenglow upgrade, cutting the time it takes for transactions to become final to roughly 150 milliseconds.

Solana is also lining up more venues for tokenized stocks. Trading platform Formation has notified the SEC of plans to trade tokenized U.S. stocks on Solana, starting with Galaxy and Forward Industries.

#5019. Nomura explores sale of crypto unit Laser Digital: Bloomberg

The potential sale of Laser Digital follows a fourth straight quarterly loss for Nomura’s European operations.

Japanese financial services giant Nomura Holdings is reportedly weighing a sale of its cryptocurrency subsidiary Laser Digital as Nomura’s European operations continue to post losses.

Nomura has held talks with potential buyers, including Marex Group, Bloomberg reported Wednesday. The company has yet to make a final decision and could keep the business, according to the report.

Nomura’s European businesses posted a pretax loss of 7.4 billion yen ($46.5 million) in the quarter ended Sept. 30, 2026, their fourth consecutive quarterly loss. The company posted pretax profits in every other reporting region over the same period. Nomura did not disclose whether Laser Digital, which is headquartered in Switzerland, contributed to the European result.

Nomura is one of Japan’s largest financial services groups, with its investment management division overseeing 152.8 trillion yen ($960 billion) in assets as of September 2026.

The potential sale comes less than three months after Laser Digital Japan secured the country’s first new crypto exchange license in four years, allowing the firm to expand its institutional crypto trading services in Japan.

Established in 2022, Laser Digital provides institutional cryptocurrency trading, asset management and venture investment services. The company has also pursued expansion in the United States, receiving preliminary approval from the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency for its proposed national trust bank in May.

During a January earnings call, chief financial officer Hiroyuki Moriuchi said the company would reduce its cryptocurrency trading positions to limit short-term volatility while continuing to expand Laser Digital over the medium to long term.

#5016. SoFi Brings Its Bank-Issued Stablecoin to Polygon’s Payments Stack

SoFi Brings Its Bank-Issued Stablecoin to Polygon’s Payments Stack

SoFi is widening the reach of its digital dollar, bringing SoFiUSD, the first stablecoin issued by a U.S. national bank, onto Polygon’s payments infrastructure as banks and fintechs push stablecoins deeper into everyday money movement.

Polygon Labs said Thursday that SoFiUSD is now live on Polygon Open Money Stack, a payments layer that bundles fiat on- and off-ramps, embedded wallets and cross-chain settlement into a single integration.

The move adds Polygon alongside Ethereum and Solana, the networks SoFiUSD already runs on, and lets SoFi’s more than 17 million members buy, sell, hold, and convert the token on Polygon directly in the SoFi app, without opening a separate crypto wallet or manually bridging assets between chains.

“SoFi is well positioned to bring stablecoins into mainstream finance because it combines the regulatory foundation of a national bank with the reach of a major consumer and enterprise technology platform,” said Marc Boiron, CEO of Polygon Labs.

The expansion lands as stablecoins move beyond crypto trading into the plumbing used to settle card payments, pay businesses, and send money across borders.

On Polygon Open Money Stack, SoFiUSD joins USDC, USDT and PayPal’s PYUSD, and can connect to the wallets, banking rails, and local currencies businesses need for payouts, settlement and cross-border transfers, opening up uses well beyond consumer trading.

The token is redeemable one-to-one for U.S. dollars and issued by SoFi Bank, which is regulated by the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency.

SoFi launched SoFiUSD late last year across Ethereum and Solana as the first stablecoin from a U.S. national bank, and it already settles the company’s entire card program over Mastercard’s network. The firm has been building out a broader digital-money suite, recently launching SoFi Earn, a tokenized deposit that pays 4.40% yield and converts one-to-one into SoFiUSD.

For Polygon, the addition deepens a payments business that has become one of the network’s calling cards.

Polygon recently extended Open Money Stack to Solana, and the chain has processed more than $3 trillion in lifetime stablecoin transfer volume, according to the company. Visa and Mastercard support stablecoin settlement on Polygon, while Stripe uses it to route USDC payments for merchants in more than 150 countries.

SoFiUSD is a payment stablecoin, not a bank deposit, and is not FDIC- or SIPC-insured, bank-guaranteed or legal tender.

#5014. Jensen Huang Resigns as Nvidia CEO, With CFO Colette Kress Named Interim Chief

Jensen Huang Resigns as Nvidia CEO, With CFO Colette Kress Named Interim Chief

Jensen Huang has resigned as CEO of Nvidia, ending a 33-year tenure at the helm of the chipmaker he co-founded, after reports of affairs with a suspected Chinese spy and a senior company executive.

Huang has stepped down as president, CEO and a member of the board, effective immediately, Nvidia said on Thursday. Colette Kress, Nvidia's chief financial officer since 2013, will serve as interim CEO while remaining CFO, as the board searches for a permanent successor from both inside and outside the company. Nvidia did not give a reason for Huang's resignation, but thanked him for his "immeasurable contributions to the company and the industry."

NVIDIA announces CEO transition. Read the release: https://t.co/MTTUvFHCJA

— NVIDIA Newsroom (@nvidianewsroom) November 12, 2026

The board also named Harvey Jones, a former CEO and executive chairman of chip design software company Synopsys, as its first-ever chair.

"The Board has full confidence in Colette and the leadership team, and we expect the company's operations, customer commitments and product roadmap to continue without interruption," Jones said.

Kress said she was "committed to building on the extraordinary foundation Jensen created over the last 33 years." Nvidia will report its third-quarter results as scheduled on Tuesday, the company said.

Nvidia shares were down 7.7% at $160.28 shortly after the market opened on Thursday, having fallen as low as $148.80, according to Yahoo! Finance data.

Huang's departure comes four days after he acknowledged in a letter to staff that he had been unfaithful to his wife, prompting Nvidia's board to open an independent investigation. He had told the board that he had been intimate with Alice Huang, an executive at Singapore-based Nvidia customer Megaspeed, The New York Times reported.

The Times had reported in October that U.S. officials had concluded Alice Huang was a Chinese intelligence asset, while the Financial Times later reported that a U.S. government memo said the two had been romantically involved. China has denied the allegations.

On Wednesday, the Times reported that Huang had also had a relationship with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's vice president of health care, who reports to him. The Wall Street Journal later reported that the board was preparing to oust him, adding to the pressure on the CEO.

The scandal has wiped hundreds of billions of dollars off Nvidia's market value, with the company losing about $430 billion in two days earlier this week. Nvidia and Huang also face a proposed shareholder class action, and lawmakers had threatened to subpoena him.

Huang ran Nvidia with about 60 executives reporting directly to him and has said he did not believe in succession planning, leaving the company without an obvious successor.

Prior to the announcement of Huang's resignation, one person inside the company had told the Financial Times that naming Kress as interim CEO would be the simplest option. Other potential candidates cited by the paper's sources include Ian Buck, who runs Nvidia's data center business, and Arm CEO Rene Haas, a former Nvidia executive.

Huang remains Nvidia's largest shareholder, with a stake of about 3.6%, according to the Journal.

#5012. Uncalled US House races could send more crypto allies to Congress

The remaining races feature pro-crypto candidates and others without a stated position, giving advocacy groups what they see as “an opportunity” for outreach.

Just over a week after a “blue wave” handed Democrats control of the US House and Senate, 14 races have yet to be called. The results so far have added crypto supporters in both chambers and the remaining races could bring more into Congress.

Three candidates in the uncalled races received backing from crypto political action committees (PACs). According to Stand With Crypto, every candidate in those races is either strongly pro-crypto or has no stated position.

As crypto advocacy groups look ahead to 2028, they’re turning their attention to candidates who have yet to take a public stance on crypto.

Crypto PACs backed three candidates in US House races that remain undecided. Two incumbents lead in Alaska and North Carolina, while a Louisiana state senator faces a December runoff.

Rep. Nick Begich leads in Alaska’s US House race. Defend American Jobs, Fairshake’s Republican-facing affiliate, backed him with $508,142 in the August primary. The same PAC put $150,600 behind Rep. David Rouzer, who leads in North Carolina’s 7th District.

Louisiana state Sen. Blake Miguez will face Democrat Chauna Banks in a Dec. 12 runoff for the state’s 6th District. The Fellowship PAC backed Miguez with $250,000.

The Associated Press called the race in South Carolina’s 2nd District for incumbent Rep. Joe Wilson on the morning of Nov. 11. Stand With Crypto rates Wilson as “strongly supportive of crypto.” His win brought the group’s House tally to 246 crypto supporters and 107 opponents, while the Senate stood at 50 supporters and 33 opponents.

In the remaining races, Stand With Crypto lists each candidate as either strongly supportive of crypto or having no stated position. “The new members that have no stance present an opportunity,” Blockchain Association Chief Policy Officer Lindsay Fraser told Cointelegraph.

Nearly one in four members of the incoming Congress will be new, Fraser said, and many have given little thought to blockchain technology. “To us, that represents a blank slate in terms of education,” she said.

Blockchain Association is planning a January fly-in to reach newly elected lawmakers. “Leaving the 120th Congress with more members in that A and B category would be a huge success,” she said, referring to Stand With Crypto’s ratings. The group gives an A to candidates who strongly support crypto and a B to those who are somewhat supportive.

Fraser said age plays a bigger role than party affiliation in how lawmakers vote on crypto. She said members under 55 are much more likely to support the industry and that the incoming class skews younger.

Fraser said she wants the industry to enter the 2028 election “with two candidates who […] are thoughtful in regards to the industry,” so the sector can avoid “living and dying by the outcome of that election.”

#5011. Urologists Have Some Hot Takes on Whether Men Should Sit or Stand to Pee

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

AROUND THE WORLD—and on Reddit—there’s an eternal debate raging about whether men should sit or stand to pee. In the US, the answer seems like a no-brainer: standing. One YouGov poll found that only 10 percent of American men regularly sit down to pee, while 31 percent said they never do this. (There’s even that viral video years ago of a pastor arguing “a man is someone who pisses against the wall.”)

But that same YouGov poll found that where you wee varies. In Germany, 40 percent of guys actually sit down every time to urinate. About 22 percent of Swedish men, for example, sit down every time, but 28 percent sit down most of the time. Entire threads online are devoted to this question, including a hybrid tactic as a compromise in which a guy pees sitting down at home but stands up at a urinal in public.

Looking beyond preference, is there a right answer to take a leak? One study published in the journal Neurourology and Urodynamics tried to give a definitive answer. Depending on your camp, the answer might validate what you know—or piss you off.

Researchers had no issue finding 52 guys to sign up for this peeing experiment. These dudes had no prior health issues and were between the ages of 18 and 39. The guys were randomly divided into two groups that sat to urinate. Then they would stand to pee. The other group did the same but in reverse order. Between each change in position was a "washout period" of 24 hours where guys did their business as usual.

Researchers tracked how much urine came out and how quickly. So who reigned supreme on the porcelain throne? Well, neither.

Sitting or standing to urinate didn’t change how much pee they got out in each session. There was a slight difference in how fast they got to max flow, though. Men were able to reach their peak speed slightly sooner when they peed sitting down, but researchers say this finding was “unlikely to be clinically meaningful and was partly dependent on a single outlier.” Meaning, one guy was pissing really hard while sitting, while everyone else peed at a similar rate and volume no matter what position they did it.

The findings are not surprising to S. Adam Ramin, MD, urologist and medical director of Urology Cancer Specialists. “If you're a normal, young, healthy male, it will make no difference whether you sit or stand to urinate,” he says. “You will have a good stream either way.”

THE FINDINGS WOULD likely be different for older men, especially those with an enlarged prostate. “Sometimes in older men with an obstructing prostate, sitting to urinate may help them to empty their bladders more effectively as they are able to generate more abdominal force to squeeze the urine out,” says Boback Berookhim, MD, urologist at Northwell’s Lenox Hill Hospital.

HEALTHWISE, NOT REALLY. But if you have a certain preference for one over the other, then there’s no harm in sticking with one position. There's some convenience with standing to pee: You pull it out, do your business, and move on. Peeing this way is “likely to save time,” says Dr. Berookhim.

Sitters, on the other hand, might prefer the position because it’s slightly more hygienic. Dr. Ramin says guys are more likely to splash, sprinkle on the toilet seat, or even miss entirely when they’re standing versus sitting. Plus, sitters might be more likely to wash their hands after every use. Men are 1.5 times less likely to wash their hands than women after peeing—probably where they could use those saved seconds.

Beyond that necessary bathroom etiquette, there’s really no other reason to switch up your tried-and-true urinary habits. Dr. Berookhim says he certainly wouldn’t tell a young, healthy guy to change the way they are using the bathroom if they are already doing fine.

Korin Miller is a seasoned freelance writer specializing in general wellness, sexual health and relationships, and lifestyle trends, with work appearing in Men’s Health, Women’s Health, Everyday Health, Food & Wine, and more. She has a master’s degree from American University and lives by the beach.

THEY’RE PROTEINS. OR, more specifically, “chains of amino acids that vary in length,” says Carl D’Ruiz, a senior manager of business development at global bioscience company DSM-Firmenich. “Peptides can be classified by the length of their chain—tripeptides feature three amino acids, pentapeptides have five, and so on—or their biological function.” To create peptides for grooming products, technicians either construct them in a cosmetics lab or pull them from natural materials such as yeast, E. coli, or animal cells.

LOTS. BUT HERE’S the thing: Because many brands use proprietary, patented peptides or peptide blends, independent research on specific products is scarce. Yet in general, there is some data to support the use of certain peptides for skin health. Three types of peptides are the most well studied:

#5005. Tether Gold Gets Clean KPMG Audit Confirming $2.2B in Physical Gold Backing

Tether Gold Gets Clean KPMG Audit Confirming $2.2B in Physical Gold Backing

Tether's gold-backed stablecoin, Tether Gold (XAUT), has completed its first full audit by KPMG, which found the token fully backed by physical gold, the company announced on Thursday.

KPMG issued an unqualified opinion on the financial statements of TG Commodities, which issues XAUT, for the year ended December 31, 2025. An unqualified, or "clean," opinion means the auditor found that the statements fairly present the company's financial position, without reservations.

Tether Gold (XAU₮) Becomes Tether’s Second Stablecoin to Complete a Big Four AuditLearn more: https://t.co/eO0asUwvlI

As of the end of 2025, TG Commodities held 520,089.350 troy ounces of allocated gold, valued at $2.246 billion, against 520,089.300 XAUT tokens in issue, according to Tether. The gold is held in vaults in Switzerland, and each token represents an ownership interest in gold on specific bars.

As part of the audit, KPMG physically counted and inspected every gold bar backing the token, rather than relying only on confirmations from custodians, Tether said.

"KPMG counted every single bar as part of its Tether Gold audit," Tether CEO Paolo Ardoino said, adding that he believes XAUT "is on track to become the first true competitor to the gold ETF market."

The XAUT audit is Tether's second by a Big Four firm. In August, KPMG issued a clean opinion on Tether International, the issuer of its flagship USDT stablecoin, in what the company called the largest inaugural audit in history, Decrypt reported at the time.

For years, Tether faced criticism for relying on quarterly attestations, which offer a snapshot of reserves at a single point in time, rather than a full audit of its finances. The company first said earlier this year that it was being audited by a Big Four firm without naming it, before confirming KPMG.

Tether still publishes quarterly attestations for USDT. Its latest, prepared by accounting firm BDO and covering the period to September 30, showed total reserve assets of $191.5 billion against $183.5 billion in liabilities, giving it an excess reserve buffer of almost $8 billion, according to the report. Tether said it made $1.5 billion in net operating profit in the third quarter.

"These milestones advance the progress towards audits across the whole of Tether," said chief financial officer Simon McWilliams.

Separately from the gold backing XAUT, Tether has also built up its own large gold reserves, and Ardoino has said it will keep adding to its stash, which it stores in a former nuclear bunker in Switzerland.

Nvidia’s board is preparing to oust founder and CEO Jensen Huang after he had two extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy, The Wall Street Journal reported.

Directors could meet as soon as Wednesday to determine Huang’s future, the report said, citing people familiar with the matter.

His potential removal would mark a major leadership change for the chipmaker, which has become central to the artificial intelligence boom under Huang.

#4999. Anchorage Digital’s Stablecoins Can Now Settle Payments on Visa’s Network

Anchorage Digital’s Stablecoins Can Now Settle Payments on Visa’s Network

Anchorage Digital is extending its stablecoin reach into one of the world’s largest payment networks, teaming up with Visa to let select Anchorage-issued tokens settle transactions directly on VisaNet, starting with Western Union’s USDPT.

Under the arrangement announced Thursday, Visa and eligible companies can now use USDPT, a dollar-pegged stablecoin issued and custodied by Anchorage Digital Bank, to settle their obligations on the Visa network.

It’s the first Anchorage-issued token to gain that status, and the companies said the deal establishes a framework to add more of its stablecoins later.

The appeal, Anchorage argues, is pairing the speed of a stablecoin with the backing of a regulated bank. Anchorage operates what it bills as America’s first federally chartered crypto bank, overseen by the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency.

“Speed alone won’t bring institutions onchain,” said Nathan McCauley, Anchorage’s co-founder and CEO, arguing that institutions want “a regulated institution behind the money,” now getting both a stablecoin’s speed and a federally regulated bank’s safeguards.

The move is the latest sign of Visa weaving stablecoins into its settlement plumbing.

The payments giant has built out a stablecoin settlement program spanning networks like Base, Polygon and others, launched a platform to help banks and fintech firms issue and move stablecoins, and has moved into onchain lending tied to its cards.

Dan Roesbery, a Visa vice president for crypto partnerships, framed the USDPT support as giving partners “another trusted, institution-grade option” for settling with Visa.

For Anchorage, the deal advances a broader ambition to become the settlement bank for stablecoins at institutional scale, not just issuing them but providing the custody and settlement rails underneath.

The bank already issues a roster of institution-grade stablecoins, including Tether’s U.S.-regulated USAT, Western Union’s USDPT, Ethena’s USDtb and others, each redeemable one-to-one for dollars. Its counterparty settlement network, Atlas, handles off-exchange settlement, collateral management and cross-border transfers.

Anchorage also recently positioned itself as the custody backbone of the U.S.-Mexico stablecoin corridor, custodying tokens on both sides of one of the world’s largest remittance routes. Backing a token on Visa’s network, which reaches merchants and banks worldwide, extends that institutional footprint further into mainstream payments.

The companies said support for additional Anchorage-issued stablecoins could follow the initial USDPT launch.

#4997. Suiet wallet to shut down in latest exit from Sui ecosystem

The self-custodial wallet will keep its API services running through Nov. 14. Sui’s DeFi total value locked has fallen more than 22% over the past month.

Cryptocurrency wallet Suiet is shutting down, adding to a series of closures and service withdrawals in the Sui ecosystem.

Suiet, a self-custodial wallet built for the Sui blockchain, said in a notice that it will stop updating and supporting its wallet, with API services set to end after Nov. 14. The shutdown comes as the Sui network has seen a sharp decline in decentralized finance (DeFi) activity.

Sui’s total value locked (TVL) stood at about $413 million on Wednesday, down more than 22% over the past month, according to DefiLlama data. Data from Token Terminal shows that Sui averaged about 128,000 daily active users in October, down from 601,000 in November 2025 – or around a 79% drop.

Meanwhile, other recent closures have also raised concerns about the costs and challenges of keeping projects running on the Sui network.

“Sui’s problems seem to mostly be of an economic nature resulting from expensive engineering costs and low user volume rather than protocol failures,” Kadan Stadelmann, former chief technology officer of Komodo Platform, told Cointelegraph. “No flaw in the system’s core design has been found.”

Cointelegraph reached out to the Sui Foundation and Suiet for comment but had not received responses by publication.

Related: Sui DeFi protocol Full Sail to wind down after Switchboard incident

Suiet’s shutdown immediately follows the Sui-based hardware wallet project Suiball also announcing its closure on Nov. 10. Meanwhile wallet provider Phantom ended support for Sui in September.

DeFi project Full Sail also shut down following a security incident involving Switchboard that caused about $91,000 in losses.

Despite the decline in active users, transactions on Sui have increased, reaching 324 million in October, up from 101 million in November 2025, according to Token Terminal. However, more transactions do not necessarily mean more users, and wallet providers must still decide whether supporting the network is worth the cost, according to Stadelmann.

“Multi-chain wallets have expansive attack surfaces, and Sui’s approach adds costs for vendors who can take their business to less capital intensive chains,” he said. “Any individual failure of a multi-chain wallet is more a reflection of the risks rather than an indictment of any given protocol.”

Sui has also experienced four network outages in 2026, resulting in around 22 hours of combined downtime, according to reports published by the Sui Foundation.

The network stopped processing transactions for about six hours in January, followed by three more outages on May 28 and 29. The May disruptions were linked to software bugs, including problems introduced by a network update, the Sui Foundation said at the time.

By comparison, rival blockchain Solana has not recorded a network-wide outage since February 2024, when it went offline for nearly five hours. Meanwhile, Aptos, which uses the same underlying smart contract programming language as Sui, last reported a mainnet outage in October 2023.

Network outages are significant because they can prevent DeFi users from trading, transferring funds or managing positions, although the Sui Foundation said no user funds were at risk during its May disruptions.

IT STARTS WITH a quick glance—a double-take in the mirror under harsh bathroom lighting. Then there it is: a single, wiry hair brazenly peeking out of your nostril like it’s trying to escape. Soon, you’re spotting strands in places they never used to grow, like your ears, and this only multiplies with time. While a beard trimmer, electric razor, or pair of tweezers can help, the best way to keep them in check is to arm yourself with a nose hair trimmer—preferably one that won’t feel like a medieval torture device.

Nose hair trimmers are specifically built to tackle those tricky, hard-to-reach spots. Many models come loaded with extras—think built-in lights, interchangeable heads, even mini vacuums to keep your sink clean. Technically, you could use scissors, but it’s a risk. Snipping near sensitive nasal tissue can lead to nicks and cuts, and as for waxing—well, that’s best left to professionals, not your bathroom mirror. Unless you enjoy excruciating pain and opening your nostrils to infection and disease.

It might be unpleasant to look at when overgrown, but nose hair exists for a reason. It acts as a natural filter, trapping dust, debris, and other particles before they make their way into your body and potentially cause infection or illness. That’s why fully removing it, like with waxing, isn’t a great idea. But those long, visible strands sticking out? They’re not doing the job any better than the hidden ones. The key is balance: trim regularly, but don’t overdo it. Just tidy up when the hairs start to show.

Most nose hair trimmers are reasonably affordable, and shelling out a ton of money isn’t necessarily going to get you the best one. Think about how often you’ll use it, and if you’re mostly concerned with nose hairs or want to use it for other things, too. Many come with multiple attachments to help you tackle errant eyebrow hairs and sometimes even detail your beard. Plus, there are quality nose hair trimmers available at every budget point, so get ready to say goodbye to those long hairs for good.

This is the Rolls-Royce of nose hair trimmers—pricey, yes, but absolutely premium in performance. Its comfortable, well-balanced design lets me use it not just on my nose, but also for my ears and eyebrows. Still, where it really stands out is clearing nasal hair quickly and comfortably. The built-in vacuum keeps things sanitary by reducing leftover clippings and minimizing bacterial buildup.

I also appreciate the wet/dry functionality—it’s easy to clean whether I’m using it in the shower or at the sink. During testing, I found the dual-edge blade trimmed hair much faster than cheaper options, like the Zorami trimmer, which often needed extra time to do the same job. And while the vacuum system is a major plus for cleanup, I did have to empty it about every four months or so with regular use.

Testing Notes: This nose hair trimmer is bulky, per se, because nose hair trimmers are, by default, small appliances, but it is hefty. It sits well in your hand and is easy to hold and grip, which is a surprisingly needed and under-represented feature in the nose hair trimmer world. It’s truly the Rolls-Royce of trimmers, powering through thick and long nose hairs with ease, and leaving your nostrils feeling shorn and clean.

The vacuum is also a very welcome feature that I didn’t know I needed until I tried it. After all, who really wants to clean up nose hair clippings from their sink? The one thing I will say is that while you can technically use this in the shower thanks to the wet/dry feature, cutting hair of all kinds is easier when it’s dry, even nose hairs. I’d recommend sticking to using it outside of the shower.

Long-Term Results: After six months of using Panasonic's Ear and Nose Hair Trimmer, I found that it trims my errant nostril hairs as well as it did right out of the box. The battery life did decrease slightly after six months of using it, but not enough of a decline to make a huge difference.

Battery-powered nose trimmers work fine if you’re only trimming once in a while. But if you stay on top of your nostril grooming (and you should—nose hair grows faster than most people think), a rechargeable model makes way more sense. That’s why I went with this one from Manscaped.

It's not surprising that the brand that reinvented the body groomer delivered the same technology above your neck with the first iteration of The Weed Whacker, but the 2.0 takes it to a whole other level.

It packs a 7,000 rpm motor—the only more powerful option is the Panasonic trimmer, our best overall—into a compact design, and the hypoallergenic stainless steel cone protects sensitive skin while trimming. That means you get a smooth cut without the tugging or irritation.

Sure, electric nose hair trimmers are probably best for daily grooming, but let’s be real—sometimes these trusty devices just can't get rid of that one stubborn hair. That's when a good pair of nose hair scissors comes in handy to take care of those last few strays.

Of all the scissors I've tried and snipped with, the Shears 3.0 were by far the most effective—and durable. Doubling as nail clippers (though you probably shouldn't use the same pair for both), these shears are sharp enough to eliminate any lingering hairs and tiny enough to fit into the smallest of nostrils. Plus, it comes in a nifty travel kit that includes a fingernail clipper, toenail clipper, nail file, and slant-tip tweezers—all of which are stainless steel and waterproof. It’s a mainstay in my Dopp kit.

Testing Notes: In theory, you could use these scissors to trim all your nose hairs, especially if your nose isn’t too fuzzy. But, honestly, they're best suited for those precise touch-ups—like snipping away a few stray hairs when needed. But either way, take it slow. As these were designed to also trim fingernails, they’re quite sharp and can certainly cause a cut if you're not careful. To limit risk, I recommend you get up close to the mirror and be deliberate, so you're only trimming the hairs you want to get rid of.

Long-Term Results: I don’t use these shears nearly as often as my electric trimmer, since they're best for touch-ups or travel, but they still cut as cleanly as when I first tested them. Thanks to their stainless steel design, there’s been minimal wear and tear over the six months I've been testing them, not to mention zero rusting.

Of course, one of the few complaints about electric nose hair trimmers—battery-powered or otherwise—is often their need to be recharged or refueled with new batteries. This Royal nose hair trimmer combats that common gripe by eschewing electricity entirely.

It works by simply squeezing the handles together, which manually rotates the blades to trim hair. The indented handles also help to ensure you never lose your grip and the tool stays properly placed in your nostril.

The Royal Nose Hair Trimmer is specifically designed to avoid irritation by enclosing blades so that they won’t come in contact with skin, limiting the risk of cuts and nicks.

Sure, the process is slightly more laborious, and the cuts aren’t as precise as other nose hair trimmers on this list, but it’s barely enough to notice. That tradeoff may be well worth it for those who are sensitive to the noisier nose hair trimmer.

Testing Notes: Given its manual design, there were times when this trimmer pulled hair rather than cut it. This can occasionally feel like plucking your nose hairs instead of cutting them, but when operated properly with some patience, it usually holds up without much pulling.

That said, cleaning was a bit more involved than the above options, as you have to pop the top off to do so. The device is water-resistant, however, so you can simply run it under the faucet in a jam.

Long-Term Results: As an everyday nose hair trimmer, this one might not be ideal, but it’s a great option when traveling. I found it can also come in handy during those ever-stressful times when batteries or a charge abruptly die.

When it comes to nose hair trimming, or any manscaping, really, the means by which blades will be brushed against your skin is crucial. For nose trimmers, this typically comes down to one of two options: either a rotary or slide cutter. Slide cutters resemble more traditional clippers, while rotary heads are the ones that look closer to a pen cap. While rotary options tend to give a closer shave, slide cutters offer more control and precision since they only cut in a straight, back-and-forth motion.

Given that these devices are made to be inserted into the nostril, most are primarily equipped with a rotary head, but some offer the option of a slide for folks who prefer the old-school feel. Of course, there are also a few with adjustments for both to accommodate the more indecisive among us.

With most products, you might look solely for a long battery life to ensure you can spend less time charging or replacing batteries, and more time using the device. However, with nose hair trimmers, there are a few other caveats to consider, which can impact the overall grooming experience—namely, the source of its power.

Battery-operated nose hair trimmers take up less storage space, as they don’t need a charging mount or cable, but will likely cost more long-term due to battery replacements. On the other hand, nose hair trimmers with wall chargers can be refueled at any time as long as there’s an outlet nearby. Plus, there are few things more annoying than a trimmer sputtering out with dying batteries, which chargers make easier to avoid. While nose hair trimming takes substantially less time than beard or body hair, you’ll still want one that has at least 30 minutes of runtime to avoid frequently recharging.

At Men’s Health, we’ve been testing nose hair trimmers for years now, focusing on key performance factors like trimming precision, comfort during use, ease of handling, value for the price, and long-term durability. There isn’t a nose trimmer out there that we haven’t gotten our hands on at some point, while also paying close attention to common pain points, like pulling, irritation, and inconsistent results.

While updating this roundup with the latest and greatest nose trimmers, I considered past favorites and emerging tools, ultimately landing on over 20 to try or give another look. After testing each for at least three weeks, I refined our findings to a final shortlist: the eight best nose hair trimmers that truly deliver on performance and reliability.

I’ll admit, the idea of sticking a trimmer up your nose can feel a little intimidating at first, but trust me, the best nose hair trimmers are built to be safe and painless. Most use rotary blades, which are tucked inside a cylindrical guard to protect your skin. That design helps prevent snags and, thankfully, those awful little nicks that hurt way more than they should.

When I trim, I gently place the device just inside one nostril, switch it on, and slowly rotate it to catch as many hairs as possible. There’s no need to push it too far—keeping it shallow is safer and more effective. I usually listen for the sound of hair being cut, and once it goes quiet, I move on to the other nostril.

Some trimmers also come with a slide cutter, which I’ve found more useful for shaping sideburns or cleaning up my neckline. That said, if you’ve got extra-long hairs in your nose or ears, you can carefully trim them down with the slide cutter before switching back to the rotary head for a closer finish.

Also, rest assured that this process isn’t painful with the right tool. Even if you have really long or thick nostril hairs, using a nose hair trimmer won’t hurt. The blades aren’t shaving the hairs down to the skin—they’re just cutting them to a length so they won’t stick out of your nose. Think of it the same as getting a haircut.

Despite their relatively low price, it can still be hard to justify a tool for such a specific issue. Luckily, you can use a nose hair trimmer in some other places. Even the simplest ones are good for ear and eyebrow hairs.

Some other trimmers also come with interchangeable attachments to help shape facial hair and trim mustaches, beards, and sometimes body hair. But keep in mind that if you use an attachment for your nose, you shouldn’t use it anywhere else to avoid cross-contamination. Even if you wash it off thoroughly, it’s a risk.

Still, others are full-on clippers with a nose hair trimmer attachment. Choose one depending on where you want to use it, but don’t try to go rogue. Stick to what the trimmer and attachments are designed for.

#4993. ‘I Signed Up for a Marathon at the Worst Possible Time—And It Was the Best Decision I Made’

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

“If you wait until you feel ready, you’ll be waiting forever.”

I wasn’t planning on running a marathon this year, let alone the New York City Marathon. Between its notoriously hilly course, relentless bridges, and the logistics of traveling across the country from my home in Colorado, NYC wasn’t exactly the easiest to take on. I’m also a busy mama to a 3½-year-old and 2-year-old, I work full time (I am the founding coach of the Ladder app and coach Team Body and Bell), and I had sinus surgery about six months ago. A marathon definitely wasn’t on my bingo card among the trenches of motherhood—but it happened.

After a really healthy and injury-free training block, I made it to the starting line. It was time for me to have my redemptive victory, but instead, I rolled up with the flu. At the time, I had no idea, and I chalked up how lousy I was feeling to the exhaustion of traveling with two little kids, lack of sleep, and all the chaos that comes with it. It wasn’t until I got home and was diagnosed that I realized what I’d actually been dealing with on race day. From the starting line, I found myself self-loathing and robbed of the marathon experience I’d worked so hard for.

But little did I know, the setbacks and imperfections of race day and training were actually going to allow me to experience the marathon even more than if I had been chasing a pace and finish time.

Between two pregnancies and postpartum periods, a C-section, and other unplanned health setbacks, it had been a difficult few years. I felt constantly defeated. Even as someone who works in fitness, I felt like I hadn’t done much to take care of myself in quite some time.

When the marathon opportunity presented itself, there was something almost rebellious about being able to choose my own hard in spite of the daily challenges that were out of my control as a mom.

As I was flooded with mom guilt, I kept asking myself: When will it be a good time to do this? When is it a good time to do anything for yourself as a mom? The answer was a resounding never. So I decided to rip off the bandaid, find a bib (thank you, Gatorade!), and fully commit to a three-month training block with a coach. (I hired a Body and Bell member who had actually trained with me since the start of the app. She is a seven-time NYC Marathoner and the most passionate running coach I know. Check her out on Instagram: @lindaleighlore.)

My life did not stop during this time. Work was more demanding than ever. We went on two family vacations. The kids got me sick multiple times. The training conditions were never perfect—but I did manage to get the mileage in. I reminded myself of something I say as a coach all the time: “It doesn’t need to be perfect, it just needs to be done.”

Let me preface something important as someone who works in fitness: endurance training was very new to me. I am a speed, power, and strength girlie at heart. The three-hour-plus long runs, pounding the pavement and moving slower, was very mentally unstimulating and out of my comfort zone.

But this new sport allowed me to enter a headspace I had never experienced before. There was something so recharging about being able to leave the house, put my phone in my pocket, and be in my own thoughts that healed me in ways I didn’t know I needed to be healed. Training did not only provide a break from the kids, but it also gave me a space to allow me to become more available for them.

In the fitness world, running and strength training are often viewed as two completely different styles of training. We have strength versus cardio zealots. But what more people need to understand is how much they thrive together.

The aerobic engine I was building with running gave me more cardio capacity for my lifts (lifting heavier felt smoother than it ever had) and all the muscle I had gained over the years made me an extremely strong and resilient runner (I recovered so well in between runs).

I felt structurally and aerobically unstoppable.

When I got to the start line, I knew something was off. I grew up as an athlete and knew what to expect with the competition nerves—but this was different. I was coughing, had a sore throat, and a raging headache. I kept telling myself it would all go away once I started moving. And for a while, it did. But around mile six, somewhere deep in Brooklyn, the symptoms came back with a vengeance, along with full-body chills.

It was way too early to be “bonking” in a marathon, and I was confused and simply annoyed. I tried to stay toward the middle of the street, away from the crowds. I purposely didn’t wear headphones to take in the crowd’s energy, yet there I was, trying to hide from it.

I crossed the Queensboro Bridge into Manhattan, where I knew my family was waiting for me at mile 17. I was so excited to see them, but I was also dragging so badly by this point, and I needed to take a quick break. I quickly took some medicine, gave some hugs, and kept trekking on.

I knew the only way out was through. I focused on one mile at a time, kept taking my gel, and tried to stay positive. Thankfully, that's the beautiful thing about a major marathon: There are reasons all around you to keep pushing. Everywhere I turned, I saw people of all ages, backgrounds, and abilities, with their own reasons for being out there. It was impossible not to feel inspired—or reminded that I was part of something so much bigger than my own race.It wasn’t until mile 22, shockingly on the Fifth Avenue climb to Central Park, where I had a breakthrough that felt supernatural—a combo of adrenaline and gratitude for what my body was doing. I was able to see my family one last time and then finish the race strong.

I was expecting to cross the finish line feeling so victorious, maybe even relieved that it was over. But I felt kind of disappointed. Not because of how I’d performed, but because this thing I’d spent months training for, thinking about, and looking forward to was suddenly over.

So let me be the first to tell you that what you get out of a marathon has very little to do with how fast you finish. And that's not to take anything away from people who work incredibly hard to get faster and faster in this sport. That's amazing! But the marathon is the great equalizer, and here's what I mean.

The marathon is hard for everyone. It doesn’t matter how fast you run it or whether it’s your first marathon or your 10th. There's a camaraderie that develops on the course because everyone is going through something so taxing together. You're all hurting, you're all pushing through, and your pace doesn't change that.

Plus, no two marathons are the same: different climates, crowds, elevations, and race-day challenges (like getting sick!). Your finish time cannot possibly capture everything you experienced out there. And it certainly doesn't always reflect the months of hard work you put into training or what you're actually capable of.

Then there's the sheer physical demand of the distance. A marathon requires so much time on your feet. You have to have a fueling strategy (salt…hydration…carbs…). No matter your pace, 26.2 miles is going to take it all out of you.

But maybe the most incredible part is that everyone out there is running for a different reason. You will see people out there of all ages, with limb differences, on wheels, with vision impairments, pregnant, pausing mid-race to breastfeed, after a weight-loss transformation. You name it. Everyone has a story, which makes the marathon one of the most inspiring environments you get to run in.

Bandit Running Women's Vanisher™ V-Neck Race Crop

My point with all of this: If you wait until you feel ready, you’ll be waiting forever.

If you want to get better at running, dabble in a 5K or 10K, or even a half-marathon. But if you want to learn who you really are deep within your core, sign up for the marathon. There's something about those 26.2 miles that shows you a side of yourself you might never have met otherwise. But you have to surrender to every mile and let the race have its way with you to truly transform.

And if you’re a busy mama like me—debating if you can, debating if it’s fair to the kids, debating if it’s the right time—there is no right time. There will always be a sick kid, a work deadline, a setback, a reason to wait. You aren’t promised to show up to the start line feeling your best.

Not because you have anything to prove. You get through bedtime every night without a crowd cheering you on or a medal waiting at the finish line. You're already doing hard things every single day. But sometimes you need to choose something hard just for you to remember what you're capable of.

And maybe the best part isn't even what you discover about yourself along the way. It's that your kids get to grow up watching their mom go after something she wants, even when the timing isn't perfect, even when it's hard, and even when it would be so much easier not to.

Lauren Kanski, CPT, is a member of the Women’s Health advisory board, a NASM-certified personal trainer, and a kettlebell and strength training specialist. She is the founding coach of the Ladder fitness app, where she leads Team Body and Bell, a strength training program focused on building muscle, power, and confidence. She lives in Colorado with her husband and two little ones.

#4987. MSCI confirms Strategy’s removal from indexes at end of November

Strategy, Metaplanet and Upexi are marked for deletion in MSCI’s final list, with changes taking effect after the Nov. 30 close.

Index provider MSCI has confirmed Bitcoin treasury company Strategy will be removed from its global equity indexes, following months of debate over whether crypto treasury firms qualify as operating businesses.

MSCI’s final list of affected securities, released as part of its November index review, lists “STRATEGY A” with the action “Deleted.” Japan’s Metaplanet and crypto treasury company Upexi are also marked for deletion, while Ether treasury firm Sharplink is on a watchlist.

Strategy shares fell 1.65% in after-hours trading on Wednesday.

The changes take effect after market close on Nov. 30, under the implementation timetable MSCI announced in October.

Removal could prompt funds tracking the affected benchmarks to sell the companies’ shares, reducing a source of passive investment demand.

As Cointelegraph reported in October, JPMorgan previously estimated that Strategy’s exclusion could trigger roughly $2.8 billion in selling.

Strategy opposed the proposal, arguing that it repackaged MSCI’s earlier effort to exclude digital asset treasury companies and injected policy judgments into index construction.

The company nevertheless played down the potential disruption. In its consultation response, Strategy said MSCI-linked funds held approximately 13 million shares, representing 3.1% of its basic shares outstanding and less than one day’s trading volume.

Related: Bitcoin think tank questions MSCI’s ‘invisible committee’ over Strategy, Metaplanet rule

#4986. 35 Best Home Gym Equipment Items to Build Your Gym, Tested By Us

This gear will make you never want to leave your personal fitness sanctuary.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

WHETHER YOU'RE A weightlifter, CrossFit acolyte, cardio junkie, or yoga lover, a dependable home gym setup is a must. You might not have the square footage or budget to create a space that replicates your go-to health club or weight room space, but you can still achieve great workouts at home with the best home gym equipment.

Building your home fitness setup should prioritize space, functionality, and usability over trends. Choose gear that suits your needs and storage space. Whether it's a full-on garage gym or portable equipment, the best home gym equipment can help you make the most of your home workouts.

Read more: How Men's Health Thoroughly Tests and Reviews Fitness Products

From traditional heavy lifting (we love these barbell sets and weight benches) to HIIT workouts (this 15-minute interval workout is sure to make you sweat) to full-on indoor cardio rigs (like the best indoor rowing machines and the best ellipticals), we've tested and vetted something out there for every type of training imaginable. In fact, we've used hundreds of pieces of equipment throughout the years, from the most high-end, commercial-grade options all the way down to budget gear from Amazon. Our extensive testing process has involved a comprehensive evaluation of multiple factors, including durability, performance, suitability for different fitness levels, and value, to ensure that we recommend only the best.

SMRTFT’s Nüobell is the perfect ultra-durable adjustable dumbbell for my home workouts. It can easily be five pounds, perfect for warm-up work, or 80 pounds, enough to challenge most people on fundamental leg moves, Eric Sung, C.S.C.S., a member of the Men's Health Strength in Diversity initiative and trainer at Performance Lab in New York City, told us.

These adjustable dumbbells give you the convenience of 16 sets of dumbbells all in one compact footprint. They're easy to use and offer superior durability thanks to their machined steel weight plates. If you're starting a home gym from scratch or live in tight confines with little room to spare, consider these a must-have. Few items pack as much versatility and return on investment in such a small package.

PowerBlock is practically synonymous with adjustable dumbbells—and for good reason. The Pro 100 model is compact, rugged, and replaces an entire weight rack. With a range from 5 to 100 pounds, it offers more versatility than almost any other dumbbell on the market.

One of our testers, Maillard Howell, who tried PowerBlock’s Pro 50 model, said he liked how compact the dumbbells were and that the square shape lets you set them down without rolling away. Men’s Health Fitness Director Ebenezer Samuel, C.S.C.S., likes how easy they are to adjust. He’s also dropped these dumbbells from about four feet and reported zero breakage (though we wouldn’t suggest dropping them).

There’s not much to nitpick with these dumbbells. That said, they can feel awkward and obtrusive during specific exercises. For example, because your hand and wrist are inside the bell, they can feel clunky during dumbbell curls. Samuel says the weight distribution differs between PowerBlocks and traditional dumbbells, and he sticks with the latter for most accessory movements (biceps curls, skull crushers, lateral raises, etc.).

We dubbed this bench the “mid-range bench that delivers big value”. For around $350, we’re confident the AB-3000 is nicer than any bench you’ve used in a commercial gym and can serve most lifters for years. It offers flat, incline, and decline options, which most adjustable benches on the market don’t. You’ll never outlift the 1,000-pound weight capacity, and the redesigned 2.0 version features a longer back leg to eliminate side-to-side wobble.

“Hands down, my favorite feature is the ladder-style adjustment system—you can drag the bench to any upright angle in seconds,” says NASM-certified personal trainer and product tester Andrew Gutman.

There are a few trade-offs. The 2.1-inch pad gap, while common among adjustable benches, could bother some lifters if their hips land in the gap mid-set. The bench also can’t be stored upright, and at nearly five feet long, it claims a chunk of floor space. Lastly, while $350 is a fair price for this level of quality, it’s not exactly pocket change.

Read More: Our Review of the Rep Fitness AB-3000

Hammer Strength (by Life Fitness) outfits weight rooms for elite organizations—from the Tennessee Titans to Team USA Bobsled. And for good reason: When it comes to quality, dependability, and customization, Hammer Strength sets the gold standard. Even the Men’s Health weight room features Hammer Strength’s Elite iD Half Rack.

The HD NX rack is highly customizable. You can choose between two heights (86" or 91"), two storage depths (15" or 21"), and either four or six uprights. It's essentially a commercial-grade system adapted for home use. That is if your “home gym” resembles a college weight room. Before buying, measure your space carefully and consider your long-term training plans. Even in its slimmest configuration, the HD NX commands serious square footage.

But with that footprint comes unmatched functionality. You can outfit it with almost anything: multiple pull-up bar variations, band pegs, barbell storage, Nordic curl attachments, and more. The rack works with a wide range of accessories and is built to withstand hard workouts year after year.

The HD NX is the best rack money can buy, but you’ll need a lot of it. It’s overkill for most lifters, but for those building the ultimate home gym with no budget restrictions, this is the crown jewel. It’s a lifetime investment you’ll never regret.

Foldable squat racks are a game-changer for home gyms, and Titan’s T-3 Series rack offers one of the best values. When not in use, it folds flat to just five inches off the wall. Unfolded, it gives you the option of 21” or 41” of depth, with a substantial 1,100-pound weight capacity, more than enough for even serious lifters. It also comes with J-hooks (essential for racking your barbell) and a pull-up bar for added versatility.

This space-saver does come with trade-offs. Like most folding racks, it requires wall mounting, and the necessary hardware isn’t included. You’ll also want to make sure your wall can support both the 145-pound rack and the load you plan to lift. Even when mounted properly, a wall-mounted rack may feel less stable than a fully bolted-down or freestanding unit.

That said, for under $400 shipped (and with a one-year warranty), the T-3 delivers beyond its price point. It’s a no-frills, budget-friendly rack that doesn’t skimp on strength or functionality, ideal for anyone building a legit home gym in limited space.

This seven-foot Olympic barbell has been one of our favorite home barbells for years. The 15" sleeves are designed with snap clips to accommodate any 2-inch Olympic plates. It's built of 110,000 PSI tensile strength cold-rolled Japanese steel with a black oxide finish, so it's plenty durable. It's durable enough, in fact, to be rated to 1,000 pounds. That won't quite accommodate powerlifters, but it's more than enough for beginner to intermediate home lifters.

Most reviewers say it feels great in the hands (even without the knurled grip), though some report more bending than expected when lifting 350 pounds or more. But at roughly half the price of most premium alternatives, it's an incredible value, especially for any moderate weightlifters looking to upgrade their home gym without spending a small fortune.

REP Fitness' rubber bumper plates strike a strong balance of affordability and durability. Built with stainless steel inserts for easy loading and a stylish black high-density rubber, these plates are designed to take a beating, whether you’re deadlifting in the garage or doing Olympic lifts on a platform.

For those looking for a complete set, with color coding for different weights, REP Fitness also offers one with five different plates—10 lb (grey), 15 lb (black), 25 lb (green), 35 lb (yellow), and 45 lb (blue)—and for the cost of $775, you can get everything you need to get started. We recommend starting with four to six plates to get your home gym rolling, then adding more as needed.

For lifters who want solid performance without premium pricing, these REP Fitness plates offer great value on the market.

CAP Barbell's cast iron plates strike the right balance between affordability and durability. Built with a precision-machined 2-inch center hole for a secure fit on Olympic barbells. The plates feature a durable black baked enamel finish and are built to take a beating, whether you’re deadlifting in the garage or doing Olympic lifts on a platform.

We recommend starting with four to six plates to get your home gym rolling, then adding more as needed.

For lifters who want solid performance without premium pricing, these Titan Fitness plates offer great value on the market.

Adjustable dumbbells save space, but nothing beats the feel of individual iron in your hands. Fixed dumbbells are sturdier, more durable, and have fully knurled chrome handles for a secure, grippy feel—especially when sweating through a tough set. They’re also better suited for circuit-style training, since you don’t need to adjust weights between exercises.

REP Fitness’s Hex Dumbbell Set delivers commercial-gym quality for your home. This adjustable kettlebell from Titan Fitness is “best for beginners” because it nails the fundamentals: It’s reasonably priced (around $150), adjusts from 10 to 40 pounds in seconds, and takes up the same amount of space as a pair of shoes. That said, more experienced users will quickly bump against the 40-pound ceiling, especially for swings and deadlifts.
