#4895. ‘The Gilded Age’ Star Ben Ahlers and Todd Snyder Know the Power of a Good Uniform

For the label’s latest campaign, the 30-year-old actor takes fall style to Scotland’s Isle of Islay.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

TODD SNYDER makes some of our favorite menswear, and for its latest collaboration, the New York brand crossed the pond to Scotland. The draw? Lagavulin, the distillery that’s been making smoky Scotch whisky on the island of Islay for more than 200 years.

The partnership marks Snyder’s 15th anniversary, with clothes that borrow from Islay’s rugged landscape. Standouts include a brown suede jacket lined in Lagavulin’s own tartan and Fair Isle zip-ups in the earthy shades of the Scottish moors. Pretty great reasons to look forward to sweater weather.

Fronting the campaign is Ben Ahlers. As footman-turned-businessman Jack Trotter on The Gilded Age, the 30-year-old actor knows his way around heritage menswear. Still, these relaxed layers are pretty easy to picture on the streets of New York. We caught up with him about what playing Jack taught him about getting dressed—and which piece he’d bring home.

MEN’S HEALTH: You spend a lot of time in period costumes on The Gilded Age. Has anything from Jack’s wardrobe made its way into how you dress off-screen?

BEN AHLERS: Jack has a consistency to the way that he dresses. As a footman, he had a uniform, and as a young businessman, he has a pretty steady throughline through his looks—a base structure with really well-made clothing and then accents like a tie or a tie pin or a ring that can allow for a sense of creative expression. I find that I like a level of consistency in my own personal dress as well.

More than anything, the greatest benefit of living inside of the clothing that Kasia [Walicka Maimone, the show’s costume designer] and her incredible team make for us every year is this awareness of the way clothes not only make you present to the world but also how they make you feel within them.

MH: Is there a menswear trend from that era you wish more guys would embrace today?

BA: I would love to see some of the creativity come out in menswear and in the accent work, like a tie pin. Some of the tie pins we have on this show are just so well-crafted and specific. The heads of canes the men wore back then also have such an artistry to them, and there aren’t a lot of avenues for that sort of expression in modern menswear. It’d be nice to see that creative voice or risk-taking come through in the subtle accents that we wear in our day-to-day life.

MH: Your role in Death of a Salesman got people talking about your physique. How did you prepare?

BA: For Death of a Salesman, I knew earlier on in the development process that they wanted to go the direction that they did for the top of the show, and so I knew that I was going to be kind of exposed every night. I really tried to go to the gym during the rehearsal process because I knew once we opened the show that it was going to be hard to stay as active—the show was just so draining.

The couple of months up to opening, I really made a practice of five days a week of cross-training, lifting, running, and yoga, and trying to keep my body as nimble and buoyant as possible, because the subject matter and the daily grind of showing up to the theater every day can really take a toll.

During the run, a lot of my focus was on rest, recovery, sauna, cold plunge, diet, stretching, because I’d already built the foundation of the physicality. Throughout the five-month run, it came down to being sure that I was healthy and recovering as best as I could.

MH: What happened between takes on the Todd Snyder shoot that we’d never know from looking at the campaign photos?

BA: Between takes, I had a blast with Boo George, our photographer. He is such a character and one of the best energies on set, and really delivered in the work. The whole crew from Todd Snyder and Lagavulin were so supportive, and it was such a fun little escape for all of us to exist on this island in the most beautiful landscape imaginable.

I really enjoyed getting to know a lot of the locals there. Many of the people there worked at the distillery, and I got to see firsthand how the whisky was actually made. People were so proud to share their culture as well as their craft with the world.

MH: Which piece from the collection would you wear back home in New York, and what would you pair it with?

BA: My favorite piece from the collection is the Todd Snyder x Lagavulin suede stable jacket, inspired by the texture and color of the mossy peat that coats Islay. It’s a perfect fall jacket, and I’d pair it with Todd Snyder’s relaxed barrel jean in khaki, which I think would really pop.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

#4893. 7 Best Faux Garlands for Long-Lasting Holiday Cheer (2026)

With Halloween in the rearview, it’s time to take down the cobwebs and inflatable skulls and go full throttle into the holiday season. While seasonal garlands are fittingly festive, the natural editions tend to make a mess. For anyone who’d rather not be tasked with vacuuming the dead pine needles that seem to accumulate by the minute, faux garlands are a worthy solution. They offer the look (and often the feel) of the real thing without the sticky sap or endless cleanup.

Fake garlands have come a long way since their humble, low-quality beginnings. Now made with premium artificial foliage and durable wire frames, some of our favorites are nearly indistinguishable from their natural counterparts. Better yet, you can use them year after year to deck the halls (and mantels, bannisters, front porches… you get it), sometimes both indoors and out. No need to strip a tree of its limbs; simply light a pine-scented candle and let everyone think you did.

There’s not much more you could want in a garland than what this single, super-realistic-looking strand can accomplish. Afloral's bestselling Norfolk pine garland is eight feet long and more voluminous than many faux alternatives. Its branches and needles are intentionally spaced irregularly to give it a natural appearance, and the wired base makes it easy to shape, drape, and arrange just about anywhere. Wind it around a staircase or use it to dress up your front door; the possibilities are pretty much endless.

For those looking for a pre-arranged garland, we recommend Crate & Barrel’s Kew Garden garland by florist Abigail Ahern. A curated selection of faux evergreen fronds, berries, and twigs combines with velvet ribbons for an English-cottage-inspired centerpiece. The decoration work has been done for you; all you need to do now is hang it.

Simple but effective, the Fraser Fir is the kind of garland that practically begs to be draped over your mantel. Constructed with Balsam Hill’s proprietary True Needle foliage, the Fraser’s natural texture and full volume (read: no bare spots) make it look so convincingly real that your friends will wonder how you keep your home so tidy all season long. It’s available in multiple lengths (including the 10-foot strand for $159), with the option to add LED lights if you're after a little extra twinkle.

If traditional greenery isn't quite your thing, consider this garnet-hued strand as a fun alternative. Made of clusters of velvety, flocked bobbles, it adds rich color and plenty of texture to your seasonal setup. Weave it through a wreath or let it take center stage on its own. It's a little unexpected, which is sometimes exactly what a room needs.

If your priority in a faux garland is a natural-looking arrangement, consider this six-foot garland from McGee & Co., which has all the makings of a woodland find. Natural-looking pinecones and delicate, handcrafted white berries dot its lush, layered swaths of greenery, giving it plenty of intrigue without rendering it overly adorned. It's a lovely option for anyone who prefers their holiday decorations a little more rustic than glitzy.

This faux garland adds bright red berries and natural-looking pinecones to its lifelike pine greenery for an overall look that feels like it was gathered on a winter walk. At six feet long, it’s quite versatile, able to dress up a mantel or wind around a staircase. A plaid ribbon makes a nice finishing touch, if you're so inclined.

Who says Christmas decorations have to be red and green? This playful ball garland from CB2 takes a more eye-catching approach, combining warm metallic tones in a mix of sizes for plenty of visual interest. It's an apt design choice if you’re planning to go full tinsel mode this season, or simply looking to add a little shine to an otherwise understated setup.

#4892. The 17 Most Beautiful Ski Resorts to Visit This Winter—Including Three in the US

When winter arrives, the world’s most idyllic mountain towns transform into playgrounds for serious adrenaline seekers. But, as the most beautiful ski resorts prove, the appeal of an extraordinary alpine escape extends well beyond its slopes. Why kick off your ski boots just anywhere when you could do so in a castle-like hotel in the Swiss Alps or a secluded Japanese ryokan tucked among snow-covered forests? Sure, the world-renowned runs are worth traveling for, but sometimes so are the ski hotels themselves. Think Michelin-starred restaurants, award-winning spas, art-filled interiors, and architecture that makes the most of its dramatic surroundings. Here, AD rounds up 17 of the most beautiful ski resorts to visit this winter, whether you’re an alpine ace, a beginner ski bum, or purely an après enthusiast.

Getting to Zaborin Ryokan is an adventure in itself, which means you know it’ll be good. After landing at New Chitose Airport in Sapporo, it’s a two-hour drive to the ryokan, which is hidden in the Hanazono woods of Hokkaido. Arriving at the property feels like discovering some sort of secretive lair from a Bond flick—a series of low-lying villas covered in snow suddenly reveal themselves. Built on natural hot springs, each of the villas has its own indoor and outdoor onsen, plus floor-to-ceiling windows and a private balcony with views of Mount Yōtei, the area’s dormant volcano, in the distance. Make an appointment with the in-house matcha master and prepare your taste buds for a multicourse Japanese kaiseki meal. If you can tear yourself away from your absurdly serene suite long enough to ski or snowboard, the ryokan will arrange your transfer to and from Hanazono Niseko ski area, just seven minutes away by car.

Modernist design meets mountainside adventure at Pendry Park City, a ski-in, ski-out luxury resort where “hitting the slopes” means basically just stepping outside. Tucked in Canyons Village at Park City Mountain—the largest ski resort in the US, with over 7,000 skiable acres spread across two connected mountains—this slopeside sanctuary is right next to the brand-new, high-speed Sunrise Gondola. After a day appreciating the powder, guests gather at Après Pendry for fondue and crème brulée espresso martinis either by the fire or outside. Alternatively, they head up to the rooftop for a dip in the year-round heated pool and hot tub, plus immaculate mountain views.

Located in St. Moritz, Switzerland, the Carlton Hotel boasts 60 luxurious suites that blend old-world grandeur with contemporary elements. The resort is also home to the Michelin-starred restaurant Da Vittorio.

The Gstaad Palace in Switzerland opened in 1913 and has catered to jet-setters and stars such as Elizabeth Taylor, Grace Kelly, and Marlene Dietrich throughout its long history. The castlelike hotel overlooks the streets of Gstaad, which are filled with high-end boutiques.

The Pines Lodge, a RockResort is a rustic Colorado retreat with ski-in, ski-out access set above Beaver Creek Village. After a long day on the slopes, guests can enjoy views of the Rockies from the acclaimed Grouse Mountain Grill.

Architect Mario Botta designed the striking spa at the Tschuggen Grand Hotel in Arosa, Switzerland. The alpine retreat, which was built in 1929, features 130 rooms and suites with opulent interiors by Carlo Rampazzi.

Designed by architect Sybille de Margerie, the intimate Cheval Blanc Courchevel in Courchevel, France, is the ultimate in alpine luxury. The resort, which is owned by LVMH chairman Bernard Arnault, is also filled with blue-chip artwork by Michel Othoniel, Xavier Veillant, and Bruno Peinado, whose Trojan Horse sculpture is seen here.

Founded by railway tycoon William Cornelius Van Horne in 1888, the Fairmont Banff Springs is set within Banff National Park and offers stunning views of the Canadian Rockies. The sprawling hotel, which was inspired by a Scottish baronial castle, includes 764 rooms and suites and nine restaurants and bars.

The St. Regis Aspen Resort in the Colorado Rockies received a $40 million makeover by interior architect Lauren Rottet in 2012. Set at the base of Aspen Mountain, the hotel includes 179 rooms and suites outfitted with Ralph Lauren beds and desks and marble-lined baths.

The ski-in, ski-out Hôtel des Dromonts in Avoriaz, France, was built in the 1960s by architect Jacques Labro, who was inspired by the work of Le Corbusier and Charlotte Perriand. The interiors of the distinctive angular building were recently refreshed and upgraded by designer Jocelyne Sibuet.

Munich-based firm Oikios Architect took inspiration from pine cones for the design of the AlpenGold Hotel in Davos, Switzerland. The oval façade uses over 790 curved, overlapping steel panels to create the scaled appearance. Inside, 216 tasteful guest rooms overlook the city—home to the World Economic Forum—and surrounding mountains.

Offering a unique combination of Asian-inspired design motifs and alpine rustic touches, The Chedi Andermatt is one of Switzerland’s most wonderful offerings. The boutique hotel is located 4,747 feet above sea level and includes a 25,833-square-foot spa to take advantage of when you’re not out on the slopes.

With rustic and understated architecture and interiors, Le Chalet Zanier is designed to mimic the natural beauty of the surrounding Mont Blanc mountain range. The resort is made up of a 12-room main structure as well as a separate three-bedroom private cottage. Like the snowflakes that top the roofs, no room is exactly like any of the others.

Located in a densely wooded area, Forestis is situated exactly where the Austrian monarchy established a tuberculosis sanatorium in 1912. Designed with simplicity in mind, the rich stone, wood, and glass of the hotel are inspired by the nature that surrounds it.

#4891. I Used to Drink to Fit In. Here’s What I Wish I Knew

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 12, 2026 | Reviewed by Gary Drevitch

“I am afraid if I stop drinking, I won’t be able to fit in anymore” is a common fear many of my clients have when they are considering cutting alcohol out of their lives.

If you have ever felt this way, you are not alone. I know that fear well. For a long time, I believed that I needed to fit in to belong, and I’d do anything I could to meet other people's expectations, whether that meant putting on a bubbly mask, faking interest in topics I had no passion for, or having a drink in my hand when I was trying to drink less.

When we live in a culture where drinking is part of everyday life, choosing to opt out of alcohol is not just a practical decision, but also a social one. It can feel almost like a threat to our sense of belonging and social standing.

It makes sense. Many of us have learned that drinking helps us fit in. Maybe you learned that sipping a club soda at a party where everyone is drinking beer makes you feel like an outsider. Perhaps you've discovered that a couple of drinks can make you more bubbly or extraverted. Or you have found that a glass of wine is the trick to faking enthusiasm for a topic you have no interest in.

Drinking is not only a way to participate in the cultural norm, but it can also feel like a shortcut to help us bring out the version of ourselves that is deemed more “socially desirable” by mainstream culture and the people around us. With the cultural and emotional meaning that drinking carries, letting go of alcohol can feel like a loaded decision that carries both emotional and social implications. This often creates what I call the social drinking loop.

A social drinking loop is an unwanted or unhealthy drinking pattern that is driven by our innate human needs for connection and belonging and fueled by the belief that alcohol can help us connect or fit in. Through repetition, drinking becomes one of our default ways to fit in, to be part of the crowd, or to bring out the version of ourselves that we believe we need to be to be accepted and loved.

For most people who have come to question their drinking patterns, alcohol is only what's on the surface. Beneath, there are often many invisible loops that keep their current drinking patterns alive. A social drinking loop is one of the 10 most common drinking loops that can keep pulling a person back to their old drinking pattern even when they want to cut down or stop.

Like most invisible drinking loops, a social drinking loop starts as an attempt to meet a deep-seated need. However, over time, as the drinking loop deepens, it can gradually move us further away, instead of closer to the things that we need and deeply desire; in this case, real connection and true belonging.

In the short run, fitting in can almost feel like belonging. When we fit in, we feel like we are a part of the group. We may feel accepted, welcomed, even liked. However, fitting in is different from belonging.

If belonging is being unconditionally accepted for who we are, then fitting in is being accepted on the condition that we act like everyone else.

Most of us can tell the difference instinctively. For me, it’s the difference between feeling at ease even when I’m quiet and having to put on my bubbly social mask; feeling comfortable ordering a hot tea instead of joining others with a cold beer; or talking about my nerdy science-fiction interests instead of pretending to be interested in fantasy football.

When we belong, we feel that we are welcomed for just being ourselves, and when we fit in, we feel like we have to perform to be accepted. I spent years confusing the two, believing that being liked meant I belonged.

Fitting in is what I call a near enemy of belonging—something that looks and feels like what we deeply desire, but can actually keep us from obtaining the real thing.

The paradox here is that we can’t fit in and belong at the same time, because we can’t try to act like someone else and be our true selves at the same time. When we drink to fit in, whether it's to drink what others drink, act the way others expect us to, or pretend to enjoy what others enjoy, we cover up our most authentic selves. We might fit in, but we feel like nobody knows the real us.

As with most other drinking loops, simply removing alcohol is rarely the answer. To break the social drinking loop, we need to learn how to let go of the illusion of safety that fitting in provides in exchange for the courage to show up as our truer selves.

Of course, that's easier said than done. When we've spent years learning to fit in, showing up as our true selves can often feel like a skill we have not yet learned. That’s why, in my 4-Pillar system, skill expansion is one of the core pillars to build a joyful, fulfilling life beyond alcohol.

Fortunately, like most skills, showing up with more authenticity is something we can learn through practice. And sometimes, that practice can be as simple as learning to say “no” when we mean “no,” instead of automatically saying “yes” to fit in. If you'd like to give it a try, you can start with my 7 personal favorite, ready-to-use scripts for saying no with grace. It works not just for turning down a drink, but for saying no to other things in life, too.

#4889. VisionQuest Reveals Wanda Maximoff’s Return in Avengers: Doomsday and Hallelujah for That

Elizabeth Olsen’s return is a major revelation.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

The following story contains spoilers for VisionQuest.

LIKE WandaVision AND Agatha All Along before it, VisionQuest turned out to be among the best Marvel projects to be released in the post-Endgame era. And given that the series was billed as the conclusion to the trilogy that those prior two shows set up, that should come as no surprise. While many Marvel Cinematic Universe movies and shows in the last five years have struggled to figure out what works and what doesn’t—and what manages to resonate with audiences over time—these shows, released over the course of a nearly six-year span, have clearly understood that the recipe for success is pretty simple: a slightly raised concept, and some characters people really love.

VisionQuest took a formula that felt like something of a hybrid of what made the other two shows successful and rode it. Where WandaVision had a super high concept (Wanda turning her world into a surreal series of sitcom references), returning stars (both Elizabeth Olsen and Paul Bettany led the show), and new characters people became obsessed with (Kathryn Hahn’s Agatha), Agatha All Along then introduced the idea of bringing in a vital new character in Wanda and Vision’s son Billy (Joe Locke) to go along with the returning Agatha.

VisionQuest splits the atom by pairing Bettany with a returning James Spader as Ultron (truly fantastic throughout) and introducing Ruaridh Mollica as Tommy, Wanda and Vision’s other superpowered son. The show’s consistently strong, surprising, and well-paced writing from showrunner Terry Matalas—to go along with fun new characters like the Paladin (Todd Stashwick) and E.D.I.T.H. (Emily Hampshire)—made it an easy, fun, watchable hit. And it helped that in the end, it came with a punch.

The show continued to expand on Vision becoming human, something Bettany has proven to be brilliant at during the course of his time in the MCU, but it also gave layers to Spader’s Ultron, proving that the franchise can allow some of its iconic villains to stick around and play in shades of moral gray.

By the end of the show, Vision, Tommy, and Billy have made it through the adventure, discovered themselves, and reunited as the family unit we’ve long known they were meant to be. There was just one lingering question: Where’s mom?

VisionQuest asks the question near the end. Elizabeth Olsen’s Wanda Maximoff was the most popular character (and briefly became one of the best villains) in the MCU in the aftermath of Avengers: Endgame; WandaVision was a massive smash, hitting during the peak of the COVID-19 pandemic and becoming the closest thing to water cooler talk material that anyone could get at the time. Olsen’s performance, nominated for an Emmy, was one of the most important reasons why.

She took a more sinister arc in the following year’s Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness, and—spoiler alert—appeared to be “dead” at the end of the movie. Which puts a serious wrinkle into the possibility of her reuniting with her robotic husband and immaculately conceived sons.

But this is the Marvel Cinematic Universe, and we’re talking about stories based off of comic books. There’s always a way.

Of course she is! Wanda Maximoff is one of the Marvel Cinematic Universe’s most beloved characters, and Elizabeth Olsen’s performance as her is truly fantastic. You didn’t think Kevin Feige would leave her alone beneath a mountain, did you?

Sure, it’s been more than four years since we last saw the Scarlet Witch at the end of Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness, but as the credits scene for VisionQuest (likely a moment taken right out of next month’s Avengers: Doomsday) shows us: She’s back. Doctor Doom (Robert Downey Jr.) picks up the bit of mountain she was crushed underneath, and her eyes rocket open in a Jon Snow–esque awakening. “Scarlet Witch, awaken,” Doom says. “Your power will be mine.”

It’s not hard to read into what’s going on here. It’s clear that in Doomsday, Doom is recruiting from some of our existing and most powerful Marvel heroes in an attempt to fuel his own takeover of the world. In the 2015 Secret Wars comic, Doom saves the universe from destruction after incursions (the collision of parallel universes) threaten to destroy everything; the result finds unexpected allyships as Doom takes his place as God Emperor. In that story, Doom’s second-in-command is Doctor Strange… someone we’ve already seen have quite the experience with Wanda (in Multiverse of Madness). Will they wind up allied once again in Doomsday?

The news of Wanda’s return also comes as we learn that her on-screen hubby will also be in Doomsday. “I got to hang out with Paul Bettany, who I love,” Anthony Mackie said in a recent interview, spilling some of the beans.

If VisionQuest was the conclusion of the WandaVision trilogy—and a darn good one—it sounds like Doomsday could feature a full-on Wanda and Vision reunion. And what Marvel fan who’s been along for this ride (and stuck it through to this point) wouldn’t be excited for that? Let’s get the family back together, shall we?

#4886. Diana Ross at Home: 10 Photos of the Pop Diva Off-Duty

As the breakout star of the Supremes and later a solo sensation, Diana Ross proved herself a force to be reckoned with. The Detroit native’s booming career allowed the singer-slash-actor to fashion her own residences in her own singular style: A statement purple sofa, a shag-lined conversation pit, beaded curtains, and a mirrored piano were among the features that might’ve stood out elsewhere, but all appeared seamlessly at home with The Boss. As she declared in her 1979 anthem of independence: “There’s my chair / I put it there / Everything you see / Is with love and care / It’s my house and I live here.”

Through 12 number-one singles with The Supremes, six number-one hits as a solo artist, a Lifetime Achievement Award from the Recording Academy, and a Presidential Medal of Freedom, Ross apparently managed to maintain a sense of normalcy in her domestic life. “My mom is such a mom,” Ross’s daughter, actor Tracee Ellis Ross, said on The Kelly Clarkson Show. “I had a really regular upbringing.” Read on for a roundup of the icon in her offstage moments.

Ross poses on a floral sofa in her Miami suite in this photo, dated March 17, 1970. It was a big year for the songstress: She performed her final concert as lead singer of The Supremes that January, and her debut solo album was released in June.

The singer unwinds on the sofa during an interview.

When these portraits were snapped, Ross was in the middle of a nine-day run of shows at Miami’s Eden Roc hotel—her official debut solo show after a preview run in Framingham, Massachusetts. “Welcome to the ‘Let’s see if Diana Ross can do it by herself club,’” the vocalist said during the performance, journalist Shirley Eder wrote in a March 20, 1970, issue of The Philadelphia Inquirer. Eder also reported that “Diana takes a long time to unwind after a performance… she screens movies in her suite almost nightly.”

A pregnant Ross leans against her reflective piano.

Ross, eight months pregnant with Tracee in this 1972 photo, leans against the mirrored piano in her Beverly Hills home during an interview about her first film role: Billie Holiday in Lady Sings the Blues, directed by Sidney J. Furie. Ross’s depiction of the jazz singer garnered her a Golden Globe and an Oscar nomination, among other accolades. “She’s the greatest improviser I’ve ever known,” Furie told The Hollywood Reporter in 2021. “Some of the main scenes were improvised…. She was the consummate pro and not a diva at all.”

The musician at home with her daughter Rhonda.

Ross lounges in her Beverly Hills home alongside her eldest child, Rhonda, in 1972. The “Ain’t No Mountain High Enough” singer’s career was launched by Motown founder Berry Gordy, and the two shared a relationship that was romantic as well as professional. Rhonda was born in 1971 as a result of that liaison, but Ross married music executive Robert Ellis Silberstein two months into the pregnancy, and he raised Rhonda as his own. The couple welcomed two more daughters together: Tracee, who was born not long after this photo was taken, and Chudney, who was born in 1975.

Ross at home taping an appearance for an ABC special.

In the mid-1970s, The Wiz star was once again photographed on the purple sofa in her Beverly Hills living area, which was complete with a white-shag-lined conversation pit and a mirror-bedecked fireplace. According to a 1972 New York Times profile of the artist, her 6,833-square-foot home had 30-foot-tall ceilings and an Andy Warhol tapestry of Marilyn Monroe. The grounds also hosted a swimming pool and a tennis court.

Ross with daughters Tracee (left) and Rhonda.

The Ross family’s Beverly Hills pad boasted five bedrooms and nine bathrooms. According to The Los Angeles Times, the property was built in 1964 for art collector Donald Factor. Because its walls maximized space for paintings, it was reportedly known in the neighborhood as “the house with no windows.” The conversation pit abutted a window adorned with a beaded curtain, as shown in the background of this photo of Ross with Tracee and Rhonda. Both daughters followed in their mother’s footsteps as performers: Tracee is an actor (who recently won her first Daytime Emmy for the program Solo Traveling with Tracee Ellis Ross), while Rhonda was nominated for a Daytime Emmy for her role in the soap opera Another World.

Ross, flanked by her daughters, cradles infant Chudney.

A newborn Chudney also made an appearance during the mid-’70s shoot, as seen in this snapshot. Ross and Silberstein divorced in 1977, and the singer went on to marry Norwegian businessman Arne Naess Jr. in 1986. With Naess, she welcomed two sons, Ross and Evan. The “I’m Coming Out” singer and her second husband split in 2000.

In 1978, a newly single Ross welcomed Barbara Walters to her Beverly Hills home for an interview about her career and life as a single mother in front of a window overlooking the backyard pool. “Her success has brought her every material comfort,” Walters narrated in the television special. “Believe it or not, within 24 hours before we came here she completely refurnished the living room.” The television special offered a glimpse of the conversation pit, now done up with dark maroon carpet and a navy sofa with white cushions.

Ross dressed to impress for her birthday party.

The “Upside Down” singer celebrated her 38th birthday with a party at her Beverly Hills residence in March 1982, as seen in this glamorous snapshot. Later that year, she released Silk Electric, her 13th studio album, and was honored with a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame.

Ross’s daughters were in attendance, as shown in this photo of her bustling birthday party. The 13-time Grammy nominee sold the Beverly Hills property three years later for $1.75 million. These days, the 82-year-old icon lives at Quarry Farm, a property in Greenwich, Connecticut. In 2021, she released her 25th studio album, Thank You.

#4885. Moving by Numbers: The Trap of the Easily Measurable

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Updated November 12, 2026 | Reviewed by Abigail Fagan

This post is part of a series. Read part one here.

In the previous post in this series on eating and moving by numbers, we reviewed many years of research (including hundreds of individual studies and over a dozen meta-analyses) on how tracking and quantification affect diet and exercise. And we found that the answer is, on average and in aggregate, “not much”.

In this post, I’ll explore a simple two-pronged hypothesis that’s compatible with that research literature, though not proven by it: that measuring allows you to change 1) only what is easily measurable and 2) only for as long as you keep measuring it.

This idea is sparked by the observation from last time that although none of the results from these meta-analyses of self-monitoring studies are particularly substantial, the biggest, clearest effect is that steps taken seem to increase while step-counting is happening. This raises the possibility that the tracking has more of an effect here because the behaviour of walking is more directly, simply, and meaningfully countable than other kinds of movement are, and a lot more so than eating is. A relatively simple machine can distinguish a step from a non-step, and once it has, then no more human effort is required: you walk, the machine records.

All other kinds of movement are trickier to track than a pace. For example, a recent New York Times article on “Why Weight Lifting Is Good for Your Heart” noted that the constraints and biases of measurement technology are one reason for the persistent sidelining of strength training in research on cardiovascular benefits of exercise: “One of the limitations of studying resistance training—and why it’s taken scientists so long to understand its benefit for the heart—is that exercises like squats and bench presses are hard to track with a wearable device. That means scientists must rely on self-reported data.” It’s frustrating to think just how much mere measurability has helped skew decades’ worth of public health advice towards endurance cardio and away from forms of movement that are increasingly recognised to offer a wider range of benefits.

The difficulty of measuring is even greater with eating than with squatting or cycling or skiing. Because you’re measuring the nutrition ingested rather than the behaviour of ingesting it, a lot more hassle is involved: measuring and weighing amounts of ingredients, calculating energy provision and macronutrient balance, comparing the amount of food prepared versus consumed. The sheer complication of committing to meaningful tracking of one’s eating is one reason why I think its cost/benefit ratio tends to be so poor, in ways I’ll explore in the next part in this series.

So the first step of our inference is that when you use measurement to incentivize change, the changes you end up incentivizing most are not the ones you care most about, the ones that will have the most benefits for anything else in your life—they’re merely the ones you can most easily measure. This leads to a second hypothesis, less directly supported by the existing evidence but certainly not contradicted by it: that these maximally measurable changes may be the least likely to be preserved after the measuring stops.

The formal follow-up data are patchy in general, and they seem to show significant decline across all the habits and “benefits” being studied; after you take away the measurement framework, things seem to revert to baseline at some point between quite slowly and very quickly!

(For example, Vetrovksy et al. (2022), analysing 75 studies, of which 24 included a follow-up phase, found that the step-count increase more than halved in a median of 12 weeks’ follow-up. Chaudhry et al. (2020), analysing 57 studies, report that within two years the increase is down to 10% of the four-month level, and by three to four years people are back to where they started. Freak-Poli et al. (2020), analysing 14 studies, report no change even at short follow-up points.)

Especially given that no other behaviours showed much change to begin with, we can’t confidently conclude anything about how the increases in step count decay relative to changes in other activities. Still, we might speculate that being guided by mere measurability entails a downplaying of other reasons why people might keep doing things: intrinsic rewards like in-the-moment pleasure, good fit with lifestyle and interests and environment, and good fit also with specific health and fitness goals.

Nothing against walking; I just published a personal blog post on what a lovely context it can be for thinking, and it can be delightful in many other ways too. But those delights are, I suspect, mostly not encouraged by the “how many steps have I taken?” lens. When done for counting’s sake, walking may foreground primarily the very quality of monotony that makes it so easy to measure.

A knowledgeable reader (Emily Nicholas Angl) shared an interesting extension of this thought: that immediate “improvements” generated by tracking technologies may have the exact opposite effects over the long term. It’s possible that where counting is strongly emphasised, there’s almost inevitably poor intrinsic drive to maintain the new habit, because the counting has been over-relied on to do all the incentivizing work—and has been applied only to activities that are uncomplicated enough to be readily measured. In this sense, the initial rewards may themselves become the vulnerability.

Looking at this research, it’s instructive to turn our attention to what’s being overshadowed by the quantification. In one paper I included in the review last time (Ferguson et al., 2022), there was a suggestion that quality of life tends to get ignored in the research because it takes longest to change. My intuition as a coach would be the opposite: that if you make changes that are genuinely right for you, greater happiness (or contentment, or purposefulness, etc) is likely to be an almost immediate result—indeed, that intending to enhance everyday experience should be a guide to which changes to make in the first place, because they’re the ones that are likeliest to get embedded and stay there. From this perspective, increasing day-to-day satisfaction is not a nice-to-have that may trickle in eventually, far “downstream” of the solid behavioural changes that really count. Instead, the very experience of having started doing it becomes the reason to keep doing it.

The absence of any mention of participants’ experiences of the changes being measured therefore seems telling in itself: it supports the idea of an overreliance on one ultra-simplistic extrinsic reward (the number) at the expense of any intrinsic rewards, and, in many cases, also of more personally meaningful extrinsic rewards (like specific kinds of ability regained or possibility unlocked). One might extrapolate from here to the benefits that mixed-methods research (including both quantitative measures and qualitative inquiry into participant experiences) could offer to medical research if it turned from an outlier to the norm.

A final dimension I’d like to weave into these speculations about why people do and don’t do the thing we’re asking them to and getting them to measure themselves doing is the question of individual attitude differences. I found myself wondering, as I trawled through the meta-analyses, whether what’s really being assessed in this research is less the cleverness of the tech in getting lazy, greedy humans to be more active and abstemious, but the pre-existing inclination of said humans to be more or less conscientious about the thing they’ve signed up for.

The differences between “compliers” and “non-compliers” (including “defiers”) are well documented as a confounding factor in health research. But I didn’t see any explicit acknowledgement of these dynamics in this literature, despite some studies finding big differences between “high-adherence” and “low-adherence” individuals (the most striking I found being Bertoli et al., 2025, where the former lost an average of 7 kg and the latter 3.5 kg over six months). As a participant, you get out what you put in—but you may not continue to once the study structures are over. And by definition, conscientious compliers won’t keep complying when there’s nothing to comply with! So if all that were driving the changes was conscientious compliance to a tenuous numerical rule, then once the study ends and the rule is lifted, the reasons to continue may seem similarly flimsy.

#4884. Andy Baraghani’s New NYC Restaurant is Full of Design Surprises

“I’ve always been obsessed with design, since I was a kid,” says Andy Baraghani. “I love how restaurant interiors can take you to a different place.”

At Ditto—the all-day café he is opening in New York’s Flatiron—the chef, cookbook author, and YouTube star has given that obsession free rein. With each design decision—from the vintage glass-prism Holophane pendants in the front window to the intense blue (tinted to match Benjamin Moore Buckland Blue) of the rear dining area’s Venetian plaster walls—he asked himself: “Would I actually do this in my home?” If the answer was yes, it passed the test.

The interior of Ditto, with Venetian plaster walls in a shade matching Benjamin Moore Buckland Blue, and Model S22 chairs from Galvanitas.

For Andy Baraghani, design is something of a family affair. His husband, Keith Pollock, is a former AD editor and now a West Elm executive. But opening a restaurant was never part of the plan. In fact, when Michael Silber, a restaurant investor behind New York hot spots like Borgo, Penny, and Bistrot Ha, approached him with the idea of a laid-back restaurant open for breakfast, lunch, and dinner, Baraghani admits his first reaction was: “I have no interest.”

It wasn’t for lack of experience. He had started his career in restaurants—from Chez Panisse in Berkeley, where he worked as a teenager, to Estela in New York—before becoming a food editor at Bon Appetit and winning a James Beard Award for his cookbook, The Cook You Want to Be.

But he bonded with Silber over their shared love of greenmarket cooking and decorating deep dives. When it came to Ditto, he says, he wanted the space to convey his personal style. It helped that he and Silber were on the same page. “Andy and I talked about styles ranging from Bauhaus, de Stijl, and classic modernism to 1970s and ’80s aesthetics from places like Italy and France,” Silber says.

They brought in like-minded collaborators: interior designer Eric Wink and architect Alta Indelman. Wink, a close friend of Baraghani who helped with the design of his and Pollock’s home, says the partners told him that New York’s much-missed City Bakery, which was two blocks uptown from Ditto’s 16th Street location, was an inspiration. “They wanted it to feel casual and approachable, with a bit of a New York diner quality,” Wink says.

Holophane pendant lamps hang in the restaurant’s front window.

The space, in a 1905 former factory (its last incarnation was an agnès b. store), is divided into three zones. In the front section, visitors can shop at a market area with hand-picked groceries. A glossy white counter with Bauhaus curves anchors the middle section; this is where customers line up, take a number, and either carry the food out or dine at laminate-topped tables under a trio of oversized custom fabric pendants. The menu, handwritten on a roll of butcher’s paper and updated daily, features dishes like pomegranate spoon salad and what Baraghani calls “the Platonic ideal of granola,” with tahini, maple syrup, and yogurt drizzled with fig-leaf oil.

The third zone, the one painted blue, features an open kitchen and café tables pulled up to a banquette that runs the length of the room. “There’s that good chaos in the middle and the back is a calmer moment,” says Baraghani.

Indelman, a veteran collaborator with New York restaurateurs like Andrew Tarlow and Gabe Stulman, was tasked with giving the space a utilitarian, high-tech ambience. She clad the walls and the open kitchen in patinated stainless steel and preserved industrial elements like structural arches and polished concrete floors.

But it was Baraghani and Silber who took the lead on honing the visual details of the interiors. “We went through 50 possibilities to find the right chair,” Silber says. The one they selected—a 1960s Dutch industrial chair, the Model S22 from Galvanitas—was sourced from Amsterdam Modern in Los Angeles.

Silber also spent hours on eBay bidding on midcentury ceramic bud vases. “They were each under $20 but put them together on a shelf and you have your own little Giorgio Morandi tableau,” he says.

White wall speakers and a French ceramic mask hang above the banquette, tables, and stools upholstered in Maharam’s Stripe It fabric.

The no-nonsense decor also features white wall speakers, created for the space by sound artist Tom Bloxam, and programmed with playlists created by Michael Scanlon of Chandelier Creative, which oversaw Ditto’s branding. But there are quirkier moments too. When it came to choosing fabric for the custom stools, Baraghani insisted on Maharam’s Stripe It, which he felt had a “Baja California” vibe. “We needed that twist,” he says. For his part, Wink specified his favorite stainless-steel toilet for the restrooms—Neo-Metro’s wall-mounted MiniLoo. “I added a custom wood top to soften it a bit,” Wink says.

Meanwhile, a pair of massive midcentury French ceramic faces that hang on a wall opposite the menu of the day are on loan from Baraghani’s own home. “They anchor the space and add a touch of craft,” he says. “I just knew they needed to be here.”

#4883. 9 Best At-Home Laser Hair Removal Devices of 2026, Tested by Women's Health Editors

Our favorites include Braun and Epilaser.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

Fall is in full swing, but if you’re like us and prefer a smooth look year-round, you’ve likely tried all sorts of hair removal tools. Disposable razors are convenient, but dermatologist Caroline Robinson, MD, says they can cause microscopic nicks and irritation. Waxing provides immediate results, but the upkeep and the pain of simultaneously ripping out dozens of hairs from our legs are as painful as they sound. Enter at-home laser hair removal devices, which dermatologists and our hard-to-please editors swear by for their legs, bikini lines, underarms, and faces.

They zap unwanted hairs at their roots, significantly slowing regrowth and leaving skin smoother. While they don’t offer permanent hair loss, we’ve found the long-term effects are worth using one of these devices. After testing them for more than three years, we’re confident that you’ll also enjoy the long-term results they deliver. Most of these devices take anywhere from one to four weeks for initial results, and up to 12 weeks for full results to show. Starting now gives you enough time to ensure that you’re hair-free by your next vacation to these Travel Award-winning destinations.

Need more motivation to start now? It’ll take four weeks for visible results to show, which means if you start now, then you’ll notice a difference before your holiday travel, with better results by the time you enjoy a gorgeous fall wedding. So start your at-home laser hair removal treatments now, stay consistent, and by the time your next beach trip hits, you’ll forget what shaving even feels like.

So what makes laser hair removal devices worthy of a spot in your busy routine? They have an upfront time commitment: you have to initially use one up to five times a week. But after a few months, your upkeep routine drops significantly to once or twice each season. They’re also more cost-effective than professional treatments. Hear us out: A laser that costs $500 is basically the same price as a professional hair removal session, and the results from that in-office treatment won't last forever, but you will continue using your at-home laser for years.

Ahead, we asked seven dermatologists about how to shop for laser hair removal devices and their no-fail product recommendations. They also answered your most burning questions in our FAQ section after our product highlights.

Meet the Skin I-Expert, a Braun laser hair removal device that we’ve been testing since January 2024. Given our long-term positive experience using this tool, we knew it was the clear winner of our best overall distinction.

For starters, most laser hair removal devices have about 200,000 flashes or the equivalent of 780 at-home treatments, Dr. Nazarian previously told us in our guide to the best facial hair removal devices. This IPL device has double that, aka 1,560 treatments, meaning the investment will last for several years even with consistent use. Each hair removal sesh will only cost you $0.31, which is a third of the price of a Wet n Wild eyeliner.

Next, it’s our only recommended device that connects to a compatible smartphone app via Bluetooth and Wi-Fi technology to tailor your treatment to your needs. Wohlner was impressed with how well the intuitive app assessed her skin tone and hair color for compatibility.

Wohlner admits that she never used interchangeable heads before because they were intimidating. However, Braun solved that problem because the app told her what head to use for different parts of her body. The software even analyzes how much coverage Wohlner needs to ensure she doesn't miss any spots. Lastly, the app has a built-in calendar, so she’ll always remember when she’s due for some zaps—something Wohlner admits can be hard to keep track of, but is key for results.

Like other Braun laser hair removal devices we've tried, this one comes in a sturdy carrying case that keeps everything neatly organized under your vanity, or wherever you choose to store it. The unit doesn't call out any specific cooling technology, but Wohlner said her experience was largely pain-free. "I felt a little zippiness here and there, but nothing I could actually describe as painful—more like a super quick, tiny pinch," she says.

As for the results, they were solid. Wohlner typically shaves her self-described super coarse hair daily until she started using this device. She was impressed that she didn’t need to shave her underarms for weeks after her first treatment. "After three more sessions, I saw a pretty major payoff,” says Wohlner. “There are definitely a few hairs still popping through, but they've grown back so slowly."

Overall, this device is pricey, but for someone serious about tackling the hair on their body—whether armpits, legs, Brazilian area, and beyond—it's worth every penny, especially if you feel like you could use a little help through the process.

Truly the only thing we don’t enjoy about this device is the price tag. However, it has 400,000 flashes—double the average of our other favorite devices—which means this Braun can easily last you 30 years. Genius!

If you can't stomach the price of Braun's latest and greatest IPL, the brand’s cheaper Silk Expert Pro 5 is hardly a downgrade. In our comprehensive test, Earley found the device to be both easy to use and highly effective.

The Silk Expert Pro 5 removes all of Earley’s unwanted hair after just four weeks of use. "I was so happy to say goodbye to my leg and armpit hair,” says the working mom of four. “Anything that saves me time—and trust me, not having to shave is a huge time-saver—is something I'm 100% willing to invest in." The ergonomic handle is easier to hold than the bulky, cheaper alternatives that remind her of hair dryers. For larger areas of her body, Earley holds down the trigger for continuous flashes—a feature she says speeds things up immensely.

Compared to our best overall pick, the Silk Expert Pro 5 lacks convenience features like a compatible smartphone app that allows you to tailor your treatments and track coverage areas to make sure you don't miss any spots. It does, however, have a proprietary SensoAdapt technology, which uses a built-in sensor to continuously and automatically read your skin tone and self-adjust the energy setting for safety and efficacy just like its more expensive counterpart.

Overall, it's a worthy pick—as evidenced by Earley’s testing experience and its popularity on Amazon and TikTok—if you're looking to spend a little bit less and don't mind sacrificing a few features.

We’ve been testing and liking Ulike devices since 2022. From the ULike Sapphire Air+ to the Air 3, and now the featured Air 10 is the brand’s latest model worth owning.

Instead of buying two devices, the Air 10 works quite literally from your face to your toes. The latest version is equipped with dual lights to zap hair on your upper lip, bikini area, underarms, and legs. It offers four modes, including a new setting for stubborn hairs. The gentle intensity setting zaps hair from the face, while the strongest mode uses high-speed flashes to speed up removing unwanted face and body hair.

What we like most is that Air 10 is easy to use and relatively pain-free. While other devices use heat to remove hair, the Ulike Air 10 cools itself down to 65 degrees Fahrenheit. This chilly surface helps lower your skin temperature to prevent irritation and burns from overheating. Maberry says the cooling tech found in both the Air 3 and Air 10 models is especially useful for sensitive areas like the bikini line.

It’s also a relatively low time commitment of 20 to 30 minutes for a full treatment while watching TV. "Once you get the hang of how to use the device, it's super easy to zap, zap, zap while you scroll through TikTok,” Maberry said in her review. Ulike promises visible results within four weeks, but Maberry saw her hair thin in just three weeks. The hair-free appearance was so dramatic around week six that Maberry was tempted to stop the treatments entirely. She continued using it for the recommended 12 weeks and now hairs only pop up every four to six weeks.

One thing to note: the built-in cooling fan is a bit noisy, so Maberry turns up her TV volume slightly. Still, the tradeoff isn’t a real dealbreaker: "I would rather have a painless device that makes little noise than a silent one that causes a burning sensation," she said. It’s also worth mentioning that this device is best suited for someone with fair to olive complexions and brown to black hair. The tech can’t accurately differentiate between a deeper skin tone and dark tresses.

This budget-conscious device seems a little too good to be true, but it earned a casual 4-star average from nearly 12,900 Amazon reviews. More than 7,330 of these reviews are a perfect 5-star rating. Not too shabby! Shoppers rave about using this IPL device on their face and body, including the ultra-sensitive bikini line.

Like other laser hair removal devices, this IPL tool features a manual mode that emits a single flash at a time to precisely target areas, like the chin, upper lip, and armpits. There is also an auto mode that emits continuous flashes for the legs, stomach, and arms. And FWIW, this device comes with an epic 36-month warranty and 100-day money-back policy, which is more than triple the regular return window of other Amazon beauty products.

The main complaint about this price-friendly tool is that it’s bulky, making it less ideal for travel. However, it does boast an ergonomic design for an overall comfortable hair removal experience. And since each treatment area requires a maximum of two minutes or less, you won’t have to worry about any discomfort for your wrist.

If you’re like us, then you’re probably a bit surprised that an at-home laser hair removal device can be so costly. However, we put this one to the test for nearly two months and saw major results. Based on our long-term testing experience, Epilaser’s effective tech, and the sophisticated design and feel, we knew it was deserving of a spot on this list. We adored it so much that we featured it as one of the best beauty launches of 2025 in our annual Skincare Awards package.

Our deputy visual director, Dangi McCoy, usesd this laser two to three times a week for two months on her right underarm to compare the results. She noticed the treated area regrew hair more slowly, and had half the amount of underarm hair compared to her left side. “At seven weeks, I’m still using the laser, but the regrowth has been so sparse I could count the hairs at a glance,” McCoy said in her Epilaser review.

Notably, this is the only featured device that use diode lasers for hair removal. As a quick reminder, using the wrong laser type, aka IPL, can cause burns in dark brown and deep skin tones. Thankfully, the Epilaser’s diodes prevent this from happening. The device’s unique laser wavelength bypasses the melanin that gives our skin its pigment, allowing it to safely remove hair rather than mistaking our skin for dark hair.

Epilaser is also extremely functional when you have limited outlets in your home or hotel room. During McCoy’s testing process, she found some of the cords to be cumbersome, so it was nice to have the flexibility of charging her device and using it cordless. It also allowed McCoy to remove hair from anywhere in her home, such as the couch while watching Uptown Girls.

OK, so what about the discomfort? Is splurging really worth it in this case? Turns out, yes! Epilaser maximizes hair removal results even if you have a low tolerance for discomfort. While no laser hair removal device is completely painless, McCoy only felt occasional quick pricks on her skin. The brand’s proprietary SPOT technology zaps up to 15 hairs per second, while leaving your skin untouched.

She was also impressed by how lightweight the cordless Epilaser felt in her hands. The device feels sturdy, and its ergonomic design enhances comfort during longer treatment sessions. Plus, this laser hair removal device looks absolutely gorgeous IRL—the bronze-tone trim truly elevates the luxurious appearance.

Given the laser’s smaller opening, you can even use this device on your face. It also comes with a soft-sided travel case with a short handle strap that’s easy to pack in your carry-on or rolling suitcase.

SmoothSkin's system works for anyone who wants something that's easy to use and doesn't require a lot of manual work or tinkering with buttons or various features. A patented sensor measures your skin before each flash and automatically selects the light best suited to your skin tone. This helps speed up the whole process, so full-body treatments take approximately 10 minutes.

It also includes a precision head to target smaller areas of the body—like the bikini line or even the upper lip or chin. The adaptable head also makes it easier to follow along your natural curves, like your kneecaps or underarms.

Like other great laser hair removal devices on the market, this one promises visible hair reduction in as little as four weeks and complete results by 12 weeks. It works so well that you’ll notice a difference after just one use, which is a true testament to this laser's power. SmoothSkin is on the pricey side, but justified by the fact that it offers unlimited flashes, allowing you to use this device for life. Overall, an excellent value over its lengthy lifetime. No wonder it earned 250 five-star Amazon reviews.

You've probably seen this popular laser hair removal device on your social media feeds, and our team says it really does live up to the hype. Nood’s proprietary PrecisionPulse laser makes all of the difference. The IPL flashes every 10 milliseconds, meaning it exposes your skin to less light that could accidentally cause burns.

Nood’s combination of continuous flashes and larger window make it better suited for larger areas, especially the legs. You can polish them off in 15 to 20 minutes, though it's harder to target smaller areas, like the upper lip. We also love the large digital display on this model.

It makes it very easy to toggle through the seven different intensity levels, and it's always clear which one you're working on. The price is friendlier than some other options, plus the brand offers a 90-day money-back guarantee, which makes this device a great option for anyone on the fence about at-home laser hair removal.

There are a lot of laser hair removal devices on the market, which is why you should consider a few of these pointers before investing.

IPL and diode lasers both slow hair growth and reduce the thickness of individual strands by scanning for pigment and targeting the hair follicle, says dermatologist Melanie Kingsley, MD. But, they each have their benefits and limitations.

IPL is the most commonly used type of light in at-home laser hair removal devices. This technology uses broad-spectrum light to target melanin, the pigment that gives your hair its color. The light is also unsuitable for dark and deep skin tones because it can’t distinguish between melanin-rich skin and the pigment of dark hair, says dermatologist Rachel Nazarian, MD. However, if you have a fair to olive complexion with dark hair, then you’re an ideal candidate for IPL treatments.

Until recently, all at-home laser hair removal devices were IPL lasers. But Epilaser has a game-changing laser for home use. Unlike IPL lights, which emit a broad spectrum of light ranging from 400 to 1,400 nm, diode lasers are unique because they use a more concentrated wavelength of light (around 810 nm). This precise wavelength means it can better target the hair follicles rather than accidentally burning your skin, making it more accessible for some people with darker complexions.

Both are effective, but diode lasers are slightly more versatile. That said, no matter which one you go with, you’ll need multiple treatments to maintain your hair-free results.

One of the biggest considerations is the number of flashes a device is equipped to deliver. This number indicates how long the device will last, according to Dr. Nazarian. "Many devices contain about 200,000 flashes, which is typically good for more than 15 years, although it also depends on how many areas you’re treating," she says. Other recommendations on this list, like the Smoothskin, have unlimited flashes, which means they'll theoretically last forever, but are pricier.

Extra features like multiple intensity modes—lower options for sensitive skin; higher settings for those who want to see results fast (see the Nood)—or interchangeable heads for precise treatment all over the body (hi, Braun) can increase the price. The amount you spend comes down to the features you want in your device and how long you want it to last.

One of the best ways to reduce discomfort during laser hair removal is to use cooling technology. It lowers your skin’s temperature—before, during, and after each laser pulse—to help you better tolerate longer and higher treatment settings safely.

Devices with bigger heads are more efficient on large areas. For more targeted flashes, opt for rigs with compact heads, such as the Iouniya Laser Hair Removal, which can be used on both the face and body. If you have sensitive skin, consider stretching your treatments out to once a month to start and gradually up the frequency once your skin can handle the laser hair removal treatment. The final hair-free results will take longer to achieve but at least you won’t risk irritating your skin. FWIW, she says you’ll notice thinning hair after your first four treatments.

Once you choose your device, know that it can take some time to see results. While every device is different, you’ll probably use it weekly anywhere from four to 10 weeks before noticing lasting results, says dermatologist Bertha Baum, DO. The final results might take longer to achieve, but you won’t risk irritating your skin. FWIW, warm weather likely won’t return until April or early May, meaning you’ve got several weeks to achieve smooth results. Either way, Dr. Baum says you’ll notice thinning hair after your first four treatments.

This technology has come a long way and, while pricey, it's a long-term investment that pays for itself. Think of it this way: A laser that costs $500 is basically the same price as a professional hair removal session, and that in-office treatment won't last forever, but you will continue using your at-home laser for years. And FWIW, we found a few discounted, top-rated Amazon picks that start at just $42, but you’ll want to hurry since these are fleeting deals.

At Women’s Health, we prioritize hands-on editor testing to ensure you don’t waste your time or money. Ahead is insight on what went into our editorial process while trying the latest and greatest at-home laser hair removal devices.

After testing these devices since February 2022, beauty director Brian Underwood, deputy deals and trends editor Eunice Lucero-Lee, and luxury commerce editor Sarah Maberry whittled down this list to 12 of the best laser hair removal devices. We also tapped contributors Jasmine Gomez, Lily Wohlner, and Brigitt Earley to ensure these devices work across most skin tones.

They all boast impressive features, are comfortable to use, and offer incredible value. Plus, these picks are FDA-cleared, so they’ve been evaluated for safety and efficacy. Several dermatologists also shared their no-fail laser hair removal tips and best-in-class product recommendations.

And because we know what it’s like to ball on a budget, we also considered pricing. TBH, laser hair removal devices aren’t exactly cheap. Many cost between $300 and $600, especially when shopping for these expert-approved devices from well-respected brands, such as Braun.

To help, I carefully researched dozens of other cheaper, yet top-rated Amazon laser hair removal devices. Ultimately, I found four Amazon picks that are aligned with expert guidance and are currently discounted as low as $35. Talk about major savings! For added peace of mind, they all earned thousands of rave reviews from real Amazon customers.

So if you're ready to ditch daily shaving and bi-monthly waxing, we're confident—based on our own testing and our dermatologists' advice—that this list contains only the best, most effective options on the market worth your hard-earned coins.

Dr. Nazarian confirms at-home laser hair removal devices are generally safe and effective, citing a 2019 paper. The biggest challenge with many at-home devices comes down to their inability to differentiate between dark skin and dark hair due to their pigmentation. Melanin-rich complexions risk absorbing too much laser energy that increases the risk for burning, cautions Dr. Nazarian. If this is you, then see your dermatologist for a recommendation on the best laser hair removal treatments and devices.

It's also a good idea to do a patch test and not expose the treated area to sunlight for a week, says Dr. Shirazi. Your treated skin is temporarily more sensitive, and you risk sunburn, hyperpigmentation, and delayed healing. She also doesn’t suggest using the laser on tanned and tattooed skin, open wounds, moles, or birthmarks to avoid changing their appearance or causing accidental burns.

Truthfully, they're not optimal for sensitive or dark skin. Many at-home devices cannot distinguish between melanin-rich complexions and dark hair, says dermatologist Corey L. Hartman, MD. Anyone else can still give them a try.

And, like with salon treatments, it's important to practice patience—this isn't a "one and done" situation. Many devices need to be used multiple times weekly to achieve the initial results. Plus, each at-home session can take 10 to 60 minutes, depending on how much body and facial hair you plan to remove. While a tad annoying upfront, this minor inconvenience has a major payoff because your hair will regrow slower over time with regular use.

The Oura Ring 5 is Oura's latest offering, and a few upgrades earned it a spot on our Best Smart Rings list. This version has no noticeable sensors, while previous models had three interior nodes that could be a bit uncomfortable. It still collects health data seamlessly.

Oura recommends wearing the ring on your forefinger, since that's where your pulse is strongest, which can mean slightly better data, but any finger works. I know a few people who use their Oura Ring as their wedding band.

Depending on which route you choose for the sizing kit, you'll use that same route to purchase your ring when you decide to buy.

Hyundai opened orders for the all-new IONIQ 6 in the UK, starting at £33,240 ($45,000), including the Electric Car Grant (ECG).

Inside, Hyundai overhauled the new IONIQ 6’s interior with a redesigned two-tone leather steering wheel, a digital side mirror, and a “bridge-type” center console that includes a wireless phone charger and physical buttons.

It includes Hyundai’s new infotainment setup, including dual 12.3″ navigation and infotainment screens with wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto capabilities.

In the UK, the new IONIQ 6 is available in three trims: Premium, N-Line, and N-Line Evo, with 225 horsepower RWD or 320 horsepower AWD powertrains.

Beautiful car, very efficient and from what I read, very comfortable. I had my eyes set on it, but the small trunk was a dealbreaker for me. So I went for the EV6, which is maybe even more of a stunner (in the eyes of the beholder) but admittedly significantly less efficient.

Thanks to its 800-volt electrical architecture, the IONIQ 6’s battery can charge from 10% to 80% in about 18 minutes at DC fast-charging speeds of up to 350 kW.

The new IONIQ 6 is now available to order on Hyundai UK’s website, with deliveries set to begin in early 2027.

Sadly, those in the US will miss out on the new-and-improved electrified streamliner. Hyundai is discontinuing the standard IONIQ 6 in the US after the 2026 model year, while the performance N will remain on sale.

#4880. Gwyneth Paltrow Is Launching a New Podcast—Take the First Look Inside the “Goop Guide” Studio

Viewers tuning in to Gwyneth Paltrow’s new podcast, The Goop Guide, will be forgiven for assuming the show was filmed in a room inside her serene and stylish Montecito home. The setting for her new venture (launching on Netflix and Spotify November 11) upends the paradigm of a podcaster on a sofa next to a potted fern.

The Goop Guide is indeed recorded inside a studio, but Paltrow approached the space with just as much intention as her own home, enlisting interior designer Marie Carson to bring it to life. “I wanted it to feel like a beautiful, elevated nook of somebody’s old stone house somewhere,” Paltrow tells AD of the space.

“If we can’t be recording in my home, I want to give guests the feeling of comfort and coziness,” Paltrow says of her goal for the studio’s design.

The catch? Carson only had mere days to turn the sterile studio into something far cozier and conducive to the wide-ranging conversations Paltrow hoped to conduct during the show, which launches with Zoe Saldana as the first guest. “We started to decorate remotely and I looked at it and thought, This is not the direction,” Paltrow says of the space’s first iteration. “And so I called Marie and said, ‘We’re filming in, like, a week and I need you to come and fix this.’”

It wasn’t the tight timeline that initially gave Carson pause. “At first I said, ‘Oh my gosh, I’ve never done a set! What does that mean?’” recalls the designer. “But when Gwyneth said she wanted it to feel like a beautiful room in her home, I thought, Well, I can do that.” Previously, the two had collaborated on a space at Paltrow’s Brentwood property, which meant there was already a creative shorthand between them—incredibly helpful when they had only days to outfit the space before shooting commenced. “Gwyneth has such a strong direction of what she wants and such excellent taste,” Carson says. “So I was able to take her notes and run with it.”

The focal point for the studio’s design is a late-18th-century Flemish tapestry. “It added life to the space,” says Carson.

The Goop Kitchen founder wanted the focal point of the design to be a late-18th-century Flemish tapestry, whose landscape imagery features a palette of muted greens and taupes. “I thought it would be beautiful because of what they’ve lived through and what they’ve seen,” Paltrow says of tapestries. “I love them because you think about all the life going on in front of these things for hundreds and hundreds of years.” To complement the hanging, Carson added a 19th-century Belgian trestle table from Meg Turner Gallery, antique chairs reupholstered in Loro Piana brushed cashmere, and a handwoven hemp and silk rug sourced from Mansour. “Marie’s execution is flawless,” Paltrow says. “She has a real knack for finding the perfect thing that has the right dimensions and warmth.”

Paltrow commissioned a painting of magnolia from artist Rob Reynolds. The sconces are from Goop’s collection with CB2 and the wicker stools are from Galerie Provenence.

A close-up of one of the podcast chairs: an antique sourced from a shop in Pasadena and reupholstered with Loro Piana cashmere.

In the handful of shows Paltrow’s filmed so far, it appears her guests (which include Rick Rubin, Ke Huy Quan, and more) feel similarly at home. “Everyone who walks in is like, ‘I’ve done so many podcasts and I’ve never seen one like this! It feels like a real room and I feel so at ease.’’’ she says. Considering Paltrow will be filming dozens of episodes inside the space, she’s happy it’s comfortable for her as well. “I would definitely live in this room,” she says. “I think about this room all the time now when I’m not in it because I’m so obsessed with it.”

#4879. Could Your GLP-1s Make You Blind? Here’s What to Make of the FDA’s Latest Notice.

For years, there have been rumblings and even research about a rare but serious condition that’s been linked to taking a GLP-1 medication. Now, the Food and Drug Administration is doing something about it.

The FDA just released a drug safety communication to warn patients and healthcare providers about the potential increased risk of developing non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (NAION) when you take a GLP-1 medication. NAION is a rare condition that can lead to vision loss in one eye, and it can be permanent.

Again, this isn't the first time concerns have been raised about the risk of NAION. But it is the first time the FDA has issued a warning about it.

Given that up to 11 percent of Americans currently take a GLP-1 for weight loss, this news stands to impact a lot of people. How concerned should you be if you're one of them? Eye experts and a doctor who prescribes GLP-1s break it down.

Meet the experts: Joseph Rizzo, MD, director of the Neuro-Ophthalmology Service at Mass Eye and Ear, a member of the Mass General Brigham healthcare system; Bavand Youssefzadeh, DO, an ophthalmologist with Cedars-Sinai in Los Angeles and a cofounder of the Global LASIK and Cataract Institute; and Mir Ali, MD, the medical director of MemorialCare Surgical Weight Loss Center at Orange Coast Medical Center in Fountain Valley, California.

The FDA's notice is designed to flag the potential risk of NAION to people who use GLP-1s. The FDA also notes that the agency will require all manufacturers of GLP-1 medications to add information about the risk of NAION to the Warnings and Precautions section of their labels.

"Patients and caregivers should be aware of a potential increased risk of NAION, a rare condition that can result in acute, painless, decreased vision in one eye, including permanent vision loss, with GLP-1 RA use," the notice reads.

The agency cited a 2024 study published in JAMA Ophthalmology as well as its own meta-analyses and retrospective cohort study in the notice. They also noted that “NAION cases have been reported for all currently marketed GLP-1 RA products.”

However, the complication remains rare: incidents from the FDA’s meta-analysis were just 6.4 events per 100,000 per year for patients using the medications.

The warning is just that—a warning to patients and physicians that this could happen, explains Joseph Rizzo, MD, director of the Neuro-Ophthalmology Service at Mass Eye and Ear, a member of the Mass General Brigham healthcare system. "Most outcome-related issues in medicine should be thought of as being probabilistic—there is a certain chance that events can occur," he says. "This warning indicates that the FDA has reason to believe, at least at this time, that the probability of NAION occurring is higher in patients who take GLP-1 RA drugs."

But Dr. Rizzo stresses that there's no evidence that these drugs cause NAION—just that there's a link.

So…why issue a warning if it's not proven that GLP-1s cause NAION and it's so rare? "The severity of a complication matters alongside its frequency," says Bavand Youssefzadeh, DO, an ophthalmologist with Cedars-Sinai in Los Angeles and a cofounder of the Global LASIK and Cataract Institute. "Even a rare risk deserves attention when it can permanently affect vision." The warning is likely designed to give healthcare providers a heads-up that it could be NAION if a patient has symptoms, he explains.

"It's their duty to report any adverse effects, just so people are aware of them," says Mir Ali, MD, the medical director of MemorialCare Surgical Weight Loss Center at Orange Coast Medical Center in Fountain Valley, California.

While NAION is scary, doctors say it's important to put the data in perspective. "It's extremely rare, but it can happen," Dr. Ali says. Given how much GLP-1s can help with blood sugar management, weight loss, and downstream health effects, Dr. Ali says that the risk of NAION is "not a reason not to seek these medications."

Dr. Rizzo agrees. "I essentially never discourage the general use of GLP-1 RA drugs," he says. "Ultimately, the risk-to-benefit assessment must be decided by the patient, but physicians should provide sufficient information to the patients to better inform their decisions."

People should stay aware of the risk without panicking, Dr. Youssefzadeh says. "It's also worth remembering that the people most likely to be prescribed these drugs—people with diabetes, high blood pressure, sleep apnea—already carry a higher baseline risk for NAION, so the risk isn't starting from zero," he adds.
